articles.body_html:
AI agents and AI coding assistants have changed how we approach software development, making it easier to turn ideas into functional applications.
For software developers, one of the best ways to improve your skills and demonstrate your abilities is by building projects that solve real-world problems and have practical use cases.

In this tutorial, you'll learn how to build a modern invoicing application that allows businesses to set up their profiles, create beautifully customized invoices, and send them directly to their clients' email addresses.

I'll also walk you through setting up Firebase for user authentication, real-time database operations, and file storage, and then share the AI prompts for designing and building the entire application with Claude Code, giving you a practical starting point for developing modern, full-stack web applications with AI agents.

Prerequisites

You don’t need prior experience with React or Next.js to build this application. However, having a basic understanding of React and Next.js will help you follow the code and understand how the different parts of the application work.

We will use the following tools and services to build the project:

  • Firebase: A Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) platform that provides the services we need for the application, including Firebase Authentication for user authentication, Cloud Firestore for storing and managing application data, and Cloud Storage for uploading and storing files.
  • jsPDF: A JavaScript library for generating PDF documents. We’ll use it to generate PDF versions of invoices.
  • Zernio Email API: An email API for sending invoices directly to clients’ email addresses, with the generated PDF invoices included as attachments.

App Overview

Before we start building, let’s look at how the invoicing application works and what users can do with it.

  • Create an account: Users visit the application homepage and click the call-to-action button to create an account using their business email address or personal email address (for freelancers).
  • Set up a business profile: After registering, users provide their business information, including their business name, logo, address, default currency, and payment details.
  • Create invoices: Once their business profile is set up, users are redirected to the dashboard, where they can add customers and create customized invoices using any of the pre-built invoice templates. Each invoice includes the issuer’s and client’s addresses, invoice subject, line items, payment details, total amount, and any additional notes for the recipient.
  • Send or download invoices: Users can send invoices directly to their clients’ email addresses from the application. Alternatively, they can download the invoices as PDFs, send them manually, or print copies for their clients.
  • Track invoices and payments: The dashboard provides an overview of invoices sent, including total amounts grouped by currency and payment history organised by customer or invoice status. Users can track invoices marked as paid, outstanding, overdue, or draft. When a customer makes a payment, users can manually update the invoice’s payment status.

Below is a video walkthrough of the application, showing its interface and key features:

Setting Up Firebase

Firebase is a Backend-as-a-Service (BaaS) platform that provides the infrastructure and services for building web and mobile applications. It handles essential backend functionality, including database management, user authentication, and file storage, so developers can focus on building their applications without having to manage all the underlying server infrastructure.

For our invoicing application, we'll use three Firebase services:

  • Cloud Firestore: To store and manage application data, including business profiles, customer information, and invoices.
  • Firebase Authentication: To handle user registration and sign-in using email/password and Google authentication.
  • Cloud Storage: To upload and store files, such as business logos and printable invoices.

To integrate Firebase into your Next.js application, follow the steps below.

Step 1: Create a new Firebase project

Visit the Firebase Console and sign in with your Google account. Click Create a new Firebase project to get started.

Enter a name for your project and click Continue. On the next screen, you can choose whether to enable Google Analytics for your project. Analytics is optional, so you can disable it if you don't need it.

If you choose to enable Analytics, select an existing Google Analytics account or create a new one. Once you've configured these settings, click Create project and wait for Firebase to finish setting up your project.

Step 2: Add a web app to your Firebase project

From your Firebase project dashboard, click Add app and select the Web (</>) icon to register a new web application.

Enter a nickname for your application and choose whether you want to set up Firebase Hosting. For this tutorial, we won't be using Firebase Hosting, so you can leave that option unchecked.

Click Register app to complete the registration process. Firebase will then generate a configuration object containing the credentials and project information required to connect your Next.js application to Firebase.

Keep this configuration; we'll need it when integrating Firebase into our application.

Step 3: Set up Firestore, Authentication, and Storage

Now that we've created our Firebase project and registered the web application, let’s enable the required Firebase services.

1. Set up Cloud Firestore

From the Firebase Console sidebar, navigate to Databases & Storage > Firestore and click Create database to create a new database for your invoicing application.

Select the Standard edition, choose a database location closest to your target users, and select Production mode when prompted to configure your initial security rules.

Click Create to finish setting up your database.

Note that Production mode initially denies read and write access from client applications. We'll need to configure the appropriate Firestore Security Rules soon.

2. Set up Cloud Storage

Next, navigate to Databases & Storage > Storage to configure file storage for your application.

Click Get started and follow the instructions to create your default storage bucket.

Important: Cloud Storage for Firebase currently requires your project to be on the Blaze (pay-as-you-go) plan. You'll need to link a Google Cloud Billing account and provide a payment method before you can create your storage bucket. Be aware that usage beyond applicable free allowances may incur charges.

3. Set up Firebase Authentication

Finally, navigate to Authentication from the Firebase Console sidebar and click Get started to configure user authentication.

Under the Sign-in method tab, enable the following authentication providers:

  • Email/Password: Enable email and password authentication. Leave the Email link (passwordless sign-in) option disabled.
  • Google: Enable Google authentication, select your email address as the project's support email, and save your changes.

Congratulations! You've successfully created your Firebase project and configured the essential services for your invoicing application.

Database Design for the Invoice App

In this section, you will learn how to structure the database for our invoicing application to ensure efficient data management and make it easier to create, retrieve, and manage invoices.

Before we proceed, it’s important to understand the three main entities in our application and how they relate to one another:

  1. User: Represents the business or individual issuing the invoices. Each user can manage multiple customers and create multiple invoices for them.
  2. Customer: Represents the recipient of an invoice. A customer can receive multiple invoices from the same business.
  3. Invoice: Represents an invoice issued by a business to a customer. Each invoice belongs to a user and is associated with a specific customer.

In addition to these records, we’ll use Firebase Storage to store files associated with the application, including business logos and generated PDF versions of invoices.

The diagram below shows how we’ll organize the data in Cloud Firestore, with the files stored in Firebase Storage.

Firebase Users Collection

When a user signs up or signs in to the application for the first time, a new document is created in the Firestore users collection using their Firebase Authentication UID as the document ID (users/{uid}). This document stores the user’s account information, business details, payment settings, and application preferences.

The document contains the following fields:

Field

Type

Description

uid

string

Firebase Authentication UID, also used as the document ID.

username

string

User’s display name provided during sign-up.

email

string

User’s sign-in email address.

business

map

Business information (see BUSINESS).

payment

map

Default payment information (see PAYMENT).

zernio

map

Zernio Email API configuration (see ZERNIO).

emailDesign

string

Default invoice email design, e.g. monolith.

invoicePrefix

string

Prefix used when generating invoice numbers, e.g. INV-.

invoiceCounter

number

Number of invoices created. The next invoice number is generated using the counter.

defaultDueDays

number

Default payment term in days, e.g. 14.

setupComplete

boolean

Indicates whether the user has completed the business setup process.

createdAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the user document was created, generated using Firebase server time.

When a user first signs up, the business and payment maps are initially empty, while setupComplete is set to false. These fields are updated when the user completes the business setup process and provides their business and payment information.

The business, payment, and zernio maps hold the user’s business details, payment information, and Zernio Email API configuration, respectively. The emailDesign field stores the default email design used when sending invoices to customers.

Firebase Clients Collection

Since each user can have multiple clients, we’ll create a nested clients subcollection under each user’s document. This allows us to organise client records by business, making it easier to manage and retrieve the clients associated with a particular user.

The collection follows this structure in Firestore:

users/{uid}/clients/{clientId}

Here, {uid} represents the user’s Firebase Authentication UID and {clientId} represents the unique document ID assigned to each client. Each document in the clients subcollection stores information about an individual client.

The table below shows the fields we’ll store for each client:

Field

Type

Description

clientId

string

Unique client document ID.

name

string

Client’s name or company name.

contactName

string

Name of the primary contact person.

email

string

Billing email address, pre-filled when sending an invoice.

phone

string

Client’s phone number.

address

map

Client’s address, including street, city, state, postalCode, and country.

taxId

string

Client’s tax identification number or VAT number, displayed on invoices.

currency

string

Default billing currency for the client.

notes

string

Internal notes about the client, visible only to the business.

invoiceCount

number

Total number of invoices created for the client.

totalBilled

number

Cumulative value of the client’s invoices.

createdAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the client document was created, generated using Firebase server time.

Firebase Invoices Collection

Similar to the clients collection, we’ll create a nested invoices subcollection under each user’s document. This ensures that every invoice created by a business is associated with the user who issued it.

The collection follows this structure in Firestore:

users/{uid}/invoices/{invoiceId}

Here, {uid} represents the business owner’s Firebase Authentication UID, while {invoiceId} represents the unique document ID assigned to each invoice. Each document stores the invoice details, including the associated client, business information, line items, payment details, and invoice status.

The table below shows the fields we’ll store for each invoice:

Field

Type

Description

invoiceId

string

Unique invoice document ID.

number

string

Formatted invoice number, e.g. INV-001.

seq

number

Sequential invoice number: 1, 2, 3, etc.

clientId

string

ID of the client associated with the invoice.

clientOrderNumber

number

Sequential invoice count for the specific client, e.g. #001, #002.

client

map

Snapshot of the client’s details when the invoice is issued.

business

map

Snapshot of the business details when the invoice is issued.

template

string

Invoice design or template used, e.g. standard.

currency

string

Currency used for the invoice.

issueDate

string

Date the invoice was created, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.

dueDate

string

Invoice payment due date, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.

items

array

Invoice line items (see LINE_ITEM).

taxRate

number

Applicable tax percentage.

shipping

number

Shipping amount. Stored in the document but not currently used in the invoice form.

subtotal

number

Sum of all invoice line item amounts before tax and shipping.

tax

number

Calculated tax amount.

total

number

Final invoice amount due.

payment

map

Payment information, including type (link or bank), link, and bank (copy of BANK).

extra

map

Optional invoice subject and reference information.

notes

string

Additional notes or instructions for the client.

status

string

Invoice status: SAVED, SENT, or PAID.

sentAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice was emailed, generated using Firebase server time.

paidAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice was marked as paid, generated using Firebase server time.

createdAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice document was created.

updatedAt

timestamp

Timestamp indicating when the invoice was last updated.

LINE_ITEM (each entry in the items array)

Each invoice contains an items array representing the individual products or services being billed to the client. Each entry follows this structure:

Field

Type

Description

id

string

Unique identifier for the line item.

description

string

Description of the product or service delivered.

details

string

Optional additional information about the item.

quantity

number

Quantity of items or number of hours billed.

rate

number

Price per unit. The line item amount is calculated as quantity × rate.

Using this data structure, each invoice is assigned a sequential number (seq) when it is created. This allows the application to generate unique invoice numbers, such as INV-001, INV-002, and INV-003.

The clientOrderNumber field also maintains a separate sequence for each client, making it easier to identify and organise the invoices issued to a particular customer.

Managing invoice statuses

Each invoice has a status field that tracks its progress through the invoicing process:

  • SAVED: created and saved but has not yet been emailed to the client.
  • SENT: sent to the client’s email address through the application.
  • PAID: marked as paid by the business.

An invoice can also become OVERDUE when its payment due date has passed without being marked as paid. Unlike the other statuses, OVERDUE is calculated from the invoice’s dueDate and current payment status rather than stored directly in the status field.

When a user marks an invoice as paid, its status changes to PAID, and the paidAt field is updated with the corresponding timestamp.

Build an Invoice App with Claude Code

In this section, I’ll walk you through how to use Claude Code to build the invoicing application using a detailed prompt. The prompt covers the application’s architecture, user interface, Firebase integration, invoice management features, and email functionality.

Before we proceed, make sure you have Claude Desktop installed and configured on your computer. You’ll also need a Claude Pro subscription or higher to access Claude Code with the appropriate usage limits for this workflow.

Install Firebase CLI

First, install the Firebase CLI globally on your computer using the following command:

npm install -g firebase-tools

The Firebase CLI allows you to interact with your Firebase projects from the terminal. We’ll use it to authenticate with Firebase and manage the project’s Firebase services during development.

Next, sign in to your Google account using the following command:

firebase login

If you’ve previously authenticated and want to refresh your login credentials, you can use:

firebase login --reauth

Once you’ve successfully signed in, you should see a confirmation message similar to the one below:

Build the application with Claude Code

Now that Claude Code and Firebase CLI are ready, you can now build the application.

Copy the prompts below into Claude Code to guide it through building the invoicing application, from the initial project setup to Firebase integration and implementation of its core features.

## TASK/DESIGN:

I want you to build a modern, highly interactive invoicing application website for businesses and freelancers using Next.js, TypeScript, and Firebase, with a sleek user interface and smooth, engaging animations. Ensure that all pages are mobile-friendly and responsive across different screen sizes.

The website should be production-ready, fully interactive, and user-friendly. Before writing any code, show me the designs for each page and wait for my approval before proceeding with the implementation.

**You must present the designs first. I must approve them or request changes before you start writing any code.**

## PAGES:

- `/` - A modern homepage with 5–7 sections, featuring engaging animations and strategically placed call-to-action buttons to convert visitors into users.
- `/register` - User registration page supporting Google and Email/Password authentication.
- `/login` - User sign-in page.
- `/business/setup` - Business setup page where users can provide their business information, upload their business logo, and configure other relevant details.
- `/dashboard` - Main dashboard for managing customers, invoices, and payments.
- Other pages as required to support the application's functionality.

## ROLES and PERMISSIONS:

Businesses should be able to add customers and create, read, update, and delete invoices associated with their customers.

Businesses should also be able to send invoices as printable PDF attachments directly to their customers' email addresses using

- jsPDF
- Zernio Email API: https://docs.zernio.com/products/email

## CODE STRUCTURE

- Use a `components` folder to organise reusable page components and individual page sections.
- Import and reference these components within their respective pages.
- Store images in an `images` folder at the root of the project. Use high-quality images wherever necessary.
- Follow the DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle to maintain clean, reusable, and readable code.
- Create a `firebase.ts` file and a `firebase-actions` file to organise Firebase configuration and the various operations required to handle application data securely and efficiently.
- You can also create a `styles` folder for reusable styles.

Congratulations! You’ve successfully built your invoicing application. Check out the live demo to see it in action and explore the source code on GitHub.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, you’ve learnt how to build a modern, full-stack invoicing application using Next.js, TypeScript, Firebase, and Claude Code. You’ve also explored how to structure your Firestore database, implement user authentication, manage customers and invoices, generate printable PDF invoices, and send them directly to clients’ email addresses using the Zernio Email API.

With well-structured prompts and clear technical requirements, developers can use AI coding agents to plan application architecture, generate components, integrate backend services, implement features, and debug code. Rather than replacing the developer’s understanding of software engineering, these tools can accelerate development and help turn ideas into functional software products.

If you’d like to explore these technologies further, here are some helpful resources worth reading:

  • Frontend to FullStack: Introduction to Firebase (Firebase v9)
  • Build an Invoice Management System Using React & Firebase v9
  • How to Build an AI Social Media Post Scheduler Using Gemini and Zernio API in Next.js
  • Full Stack Software Development Projects

Thank you for reading!

articles.title: How to Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) to Linear's Cloud Coding Agent
articles.description: On November 12, 2026, Linear shipped Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) for its cloud coding agent. If your...
articles.body_html:
On November 12, 2026, Linear shipped Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) for its cloud coding agent. If your company already pays OpenAI or Anthropic directly, or gets models through a gateway like OpenRouter or AWS Bedrock, you can now point Linear's agent at that account. You keep your negotiated rates and existing credits instead of buying model usage through Linear.

There's one catch the announcement mentions only briefly: BYOK covers the model, not the machine. Every agent session still runs in a Linear-hosted sandbox, and that sandbox is billed in Linear AI credits whatever key you use.

This guide walks through the setup, the settings that can trip you up, what the sandbox actually costs, and an option for teams that would rather run agents on hardware they already have.

What BYOK changes, and what it doesn't

A cloud coding agent session in Linear has two costs:

  1. Model tokens: the LLM calls the agent makes while it reads code, plans and writes changes.
  2. Sandbox runtime: the cloud machine the agent runs on while it clones your repo, installs dependencies and runs commands.

Before BYOK, both came out of your Linear AI credits. With BYOK on, your provider bills you for tokens directly. Sandbox runtime still comes out of Linear AI credits, so your workspace needs a credit balance even with BYOK turned on.

You can connect through:

  • OpenAI
  • Anthropic
  • AWS Bedrock
  • Azure OpenAI
  • Claude in Microsoft Foundry
  • OpenRouter
  • Vercel
  • Any gateway that supports the OpenAI Responses API or the Anthropic Messages API

One thing to know up front: you need an API key. A ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro/Max subscription won't work here.

What you need before you start

  • A Linear workspace on a current plan (Free, Basic, Business or Enterprise). Legacy plans don't support the coding agent or BYOK.
  • Owner or admin access in Linear.
  • GitHub organization owner access, to turn the cloud coding agent on.
  • An API key from your provider, or an Anthropic organization where you have the Owner, Admin or Billing role.
  • A Linear AI credit balance for sandbox runtime.

Only one admin needs to set this up. Everyone in the workspace then uses that connection, and members don't need their own keys.

Step 1: Turn on the cloud coding agent

If your workspace isn't using the agent yet, go to Settings > AI & agents > Cloud coding agent and set the dropdown to Enabled. On Enterprise you can pick Enabled for teams… to roll it out to some teams first.

Then create an environment under Workspace settings > Linear Code > Environments. An environment holds one repository, and that repository has to be available through your workspace's GitHub integration.

Step 2: Open the Inference settings

Go to Settings > Linear Code. Below Agent configuration you'll find an Inference section with two rows:

  • Anthropic, which powers Claude Code
  • OpenAI, which powers Codex

Each row starts on Linear credits. You can switch one row to your own key and leave the other on Linear credits, or switch both.

Step 3a: Connect Anthropic

You get three options on the Anthropic row.

Anthropic organization. Choose it, select Continue, sign in to Anthropic, pick your organization and approve. There's no key to copy and paste. Two conditions apply:

  • Anthropic has to bill the organization directly, not through AWS, Google Cloud or Azure.
  • The person approving needs the Owner, Admin or Billing role in that organization.

You manage spend limits for this connection in the Claude Console under Connected platforms.

Cloud provider. Choose Amazon Bedrock from Provider, then enter your AWS region and API key.

Custom endpoint. Enter an Endpoint URL and an API key. Use this for a gateway such as OpenRouter or Vercel, or an internal proxy. The endpoint has to speak the Anthropic Messages API.

Step 3b: Connect OpenAI

On the OpenAI row, select OpenAI API key, then Add OpenAI API key.

  • To connect to OpenAI directly, choose OpenAI from Provider, paste your API key and select Save.
  • To use a gateway or Azure OpenAI, choose Custom endpoint and enter the Endpoint URL and API key. The endpoint has to support the OpenAI Responses API.

Step 4: Test the connection

For any connection that uses an API key, select Test connection before Save. A typo in the endpoint URL is much easier to catch here than halfway through someone's coding session.

Step 5: Pick the model

The workspace model is set in Cloud coding agent settings, and it applies to all coding work in the workspace from then on. The default, Auto, currently resolves to GPT-6 Sol. You can also pin a specific model:

  • Anthropic: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5
  • OpenAI: GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4

If you've only connected one provider, pick a model from that provider. Otherwise the agent's usage will still go through Linear credits.

Gotchas worth knowing before you switch

These come straight from Linear's docs, and they're easy to miss.

  • There's no fallback for a Claude organization. If you connect an Anthropic organization and it hits its spend limit, Linear won't fall back to Linear credits. Coding work stops until an admin raises the limit. Set the limit with that in mind.
  • Provider changes only apply to new sessions. Sessions that are already running keep their original provider. If you rotate or revoke the old key, those sessions can't resume, so keep it valid until they finish.
  • Environment variables are visible to the agent. Only variables marked Secret are hidden, and those are only available while the sandbox is being prepared.
  • GitHub IP allow lists. If your GitHub organization uses one, you have to allow the cloud coding agent's IPs.
  • You can switch back at any time. Set either row back to Linear credits in Settings > Linear Code.

The part BYOK doesn't cover: sandbox runtime

This is the cost that stays with Linear. Sandbox runtime is billed in 5-minute increments, and bigger sandboxes use more credits for the same time:

CPU Memory Per 5 minutes Per hour
1 vCPU 8 GB $0.03125 $0.375
2 vCPUs 16 GB $0.0625 $0.75
4 vCPUs 32 GB $0.125 $1.50
8 vCPUs 64 GB $0.25 $3.00

Per-hour figures are the 5-minute rate × 12. Rates are from Linear's AI credits docs as of November 2026.

You choose the sandbox size under Configure an environment, and the change only applies to new sessions.

For one developer trying the agent out now and then, these numbers are small. They add up once the agent is part of daily work. Say a team runs 15 sessions a day, each about 25 minutes, on a 2 vCPU sandbox. That's 75 increments a day, or about $4.69 a day, which comes to about $103 a month over 22 working days. That's on top of the model tokens your provider now bills you for. A repo that needs the 8 vCPU sandbox for its build quadruples that.

It isn't a big number for most companies, and you get a managed, isolated machine for it. But if the reason you turned on BYOK was to stop paying twice for AI, you're still paying twice, just less.

Another option: run agents on machines you already have

If your team already has capable laptops, a spare office workstation or a cloud VM you pay for anyway, there's a different setup to consider: let agents run on those machines instead of a rented sandbox.

Sharkly.ai works this way. It's a shared workspace where people and AI coding agents are assigned tasks from the same board. Agents run on Computers you connect: your own laptop, an office machine, a cloud server, a VM or a Docker container, on Windows, Mac or Linux. There's no hosted sandbox, so there's no runtime meter.

The model side is BYOK too, and it's looser than Linear's. Agents run on the coding plan or API key you already have for tools like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. So if your developers already pay for a Claude Code or Codex subscription, the agent can use that, while Linear asks for an API key.

If you don't want to leave Linear, you don't have to. According to Sharkly's site, it can two-way sync with Linear (as well as Jira, Asana, GitHub Issues, GitLab Issues and Shortcut). Your issues stay in Linear, and the agent work runs on your own hardware.

What you get besides skipping the meter

The cost difference is what started this comparison, but most of what Sharkly does is about working with agents as part of the team.

  • Agents are teammates on the board. An Agent takes assigned Tasks, writes comments, updates the Task's status and leaves an execution trace. People, Agents and Crews can all be assignees, so assigning work to an agent looks the same as assigning it to a person.
  • You pick the model per Agent, and per Task. By default an Agent uses its Runtime's model. You can choose another from that Runtime's model list, or set a different model for a single Task. Hard bugs can go to your strongest model while routine work stays on a cheaper one.
  • Instructions and Skills you write once. An Agent's instructions go into every run: its scope, when to ask for input, how to report. Reusable procedures live in Skills, which can be shared across a Space.
  • Crews for work that needs more than one agent. A Crew is a group of people and Agents with a leader Agent. Assign it a Task and the leader starts first, then either does the work or @ mentions the other Agents. Their results land in the Task's chat.
  • Follow-ups happen in the Task. If a result is off, @ mention the Agent in a comment and it continues on the same Task. A plain comment doesn't start a run, so people can discuss a Task without kicking off agent work by accident.
  • Git history that shows who did what. Isolated runs commit to a branch named sharkly-agent/<agent>/<task-identifier>. By default, commits name both the person who triggered the run and the Agent, with a Co-authored-by trailer.

Setting it up

  1. Install and sign in to a coding tool on the machine that will do the work, such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini or Pi Agent.
  2. Connect the Computer. In Sharkly, open the Computers page, create a one-time install token, then run this on the machine: 
   sharkly computer register --install-token <install-token>

This registers the machine and starts a small local service. The service connects outward to Sharkly, so you don't need to open any inbound ports. It then detects which coding tools are installed. (The desktop app can do this step for you during sign-up.)

  1. Create an Agent. Open Agents > New Agent, choose Code development, point it at a repo (automatic Git cloning or a local directory) and select your Computer.
  2. Assign a Task. Set the Agent as the Assignee, the same way you'd assign a teammate. Assigning it starts the run.
  3. Review. The execution log shows what the agent is doing, its conclusions and blockers show up as comments, and anything that needs you lands in Inbox. Each run gets its own git worktree, so agents working in parallel don't overwrite each other's changes.

What happens during a run

A run brings together three things: the Task, the Agent assigned to it, and a Runtime (a coding tool like Claude Code) on one of your connected Computers. The Task stays the shared record that people and agents both work from.

  • The Agent gets the full context. Each run receives the Task details, the statuses it's allowed to use, the Agent's instructions, its Skills, the repositories and the environment settings.
  • Backlog is a safe parking spot. Assigning a Task that's still in Backlog doesn't start anything. The run starts when you move the Task out of Backlog.
  • Queued runs wait for the machine. If the Computer is busy or offline, the run shows as Queued with the reason, and it starts once the blocker clears. You don't need to retry it.
  • Parallel work doesn't collide. Different Tasks can run side by side, each in its own worktree. If an Agent works directly in a folder instead, runs in that folder take turns.
  • Problems come to you. Failed and blocked runs land in the Inbox, and the execution log shows what went wrong.

Sharkly is free for teams of up to 5 people with the full product. After that, the Team plan is $7 per user per month. Compute and models are on you, and that's the point.

The trade-off

Running on your own machines isn't free in every sense:

  • The machine has to be on. If the agent's laptop goes to sleep, its runs sit in the queue. They wait up to 24 hours by default, then fail. For agents that keep going overnight, use an always-on office machine or a cheap VM.
  • You own the environment. Repos, credentials and dependencies have to be set up on that machine. A managed sandbox does this for you.
  • Isolation is your call. A Linear sandbox is a fresh machine each time. On your own hardware, the agent works in a git worktree on a real computer, so think about which machine you connect and what it can reach.

Which one fits your team

Linear cloud agent + BYOK Sharkly
Model billing Your provider (API key) Your provider (API key or existing coding plan)
Where the agent runs Linear-hosted sandbox Your laptop, server, VM or Docker
Runtime cost Linear AI credits, billed in 5-minute increments None from Sharkly (you pay for your own hardware)
Setup effort Low: managed environment Medium: you prepare the machine
Agents Claude Code, Codex Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, Pi and others
Issue tracker Linear Sharkly's board, with two-way sync to Linear, Jira and others

Stick with Linear's cloud agent + BYOK if you want zero environment setup, your team lives in Linear, and the sandbox bill is small next to your token spend.

Look at Sharkly if you have hardware sitting idle, you want agents to use the subscriptions your developers already pay for, or you want people and agents on one shared board without a per-minute meter.

FAQ

Can I use my ChatGPT or Claude subscription with Linear's BYOK? No. Linear needs a provider API key or a connected Anthropic organization.

Does BYOK make Linear's coding agent free? No. Your provider bills model tokens, and sandbox runtime still uses Linear AI credits.

Can I use OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway? Yes. Use Custom endpoint on the row that matches the API format your gateway speaks: Anthropic Messages API or OpenAI Responses API.

What happens if my Anthropic spend limit runs out? Coding work stops until an admin raises the limit in the Claude Console. Linear doesn't fall back to Linear credits for a Claude organization connection.

Do all members need their own key? No. One admin sets it up for the whole workspace.

Wrapping up

BYOK is a good change. It lets teams with existing provider deals use them inside Linear, and setup takes a few minutes. Just budget for what it leaves out: the sandbox still runs on Linear's meter. If that matters for your team, running agents on machines you already own is a real alternative, and with Linear sync you can keep your issues where they are.

articles.title: Idempotency Keys Explained: Build a Payment Endpoint That Survives Retries
articles.description: Why double charges happen, the exact contract that prevents them, and working code you can adapt.  A...
articles.body_html:
Why double charges happen, the exact contract that prevents them, and working code you can adapt.

A customer taps “Pay.” The request reaches your server, the payment is recorded, but the response is lost on a flaky mobile connection. The app times out and retries. Your server sees a brand new request and charges the customer again.

This is one of the most common API design interview questions, and one of the most common production bugs. The fix is a small idea called an idempotency key. In this post you will learn the contract, then build a working version with PostgreSQL and Python.

Idempotent, in One Sentence

An operation is idempotent if doing it many times has the same effect as doing it once.

In HTTP, GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent. POST is not, because posting twice usually creates two things. Payments, orders and transfers are almost always POSTs, so they need extra protection.

The Contract

The client generates a unique key (a UUID works well) for each logical operation and sends it in a header:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 4d7a6c1e-9f0b-4f6e-8a55-1c2d3e4f5a6b
Content-Type: application/json

{"customer_id": 17, "amount_cents": 2000, "currency": "usd"}

The server then follows these rules:

1.First time this key is seen: Do the work, save the result with the key, and return it.

2.Same key, same request body: Do not repeat the work; return the saved result.

3.Same key, different request body: Reject with 422.

4.Same key while the first request is still running: Wait for it, or return 409 Conflict.

The client reuses the same key on every retry of the same action, and creates a new key for each new action.

The Table

We store each key together with a fingerprint of the request and the saved response:

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash  TEXT NOT NULL,
  response_code INT,
  response_body JSONB,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_cents INT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_cents > 0),
  currency     CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The PRIMARY KEY on key does the hard part for us: the database itself guarantees that a key can only be inserted once, even if two requests arrive at the same instant.

The Handler
Here is the core logic using psycopg2. The key trick is to claim the key and do the work inside one transaction.

import hashlib
import json

def create_payment(conn, idem_key, payload):
    request_hash = hashlib.sha256(
        json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()
    ).hexdigest()

    with conn:                       # one transaction: commit on success, rollback on error
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            # 1. Try to claim the key.
            cur.execute(
                """INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash)
                   VALUES (%s, %s)
                   ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
                   RETURNING key""",
                (idem_key, request_hash),
            )

            if cur.fetchone() is None:
                # 2. Key already used: replay or reject.
                cur.execute(
                    "SELECT request_hash, response_code, response_body "
                    "FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = %s",
                    (idem_key,),
                )
                saved_hash, code, body = cur.fetchone()
                if saved_hash != request_hash:
                    return 422, {"error": "Idempotency-Key reused with a different request"}
                return code, body

            # 3. First time: do the real work.
            cur.execute(
                "INSERT INTO payments (customer_id, amount_cents, currency) "
                "VALUES (%s, %s, %s) RETURNING id",
                (payload["customer_id"], payload["amount_cents"], payload["currency"]),
            )
            payment_id = cur.fetchone()[0]
            response = {"payment_id": payment_id, "status": "succeeded"}

            # 4. Save the response with the key.
            cur.execute(
                "UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response_code = 201, response_body = %s "
                "WHERE key = %s",
                (json.dumps(response), idem_key),
            )
            return 201, response

What Happens When You Call It Twice

create_payment(conn, "4d7a...", {...})  ->  (201, {"payment_id": 1, "status": "succeeded"})
create_payment(conn, "4d7a...", {...})  ->  (201, {"payment_id": 1, "status": "succeeded"})   # replayed, no new row
create_payment(conn, "4d7a...", {amount changed})  ->  (422, {"error": "...reused..."})

The payments table has exactly one row. The retry got the original answer back.

The Subtle Case: Two Requests at the Same Moment

Suppose the client’s retry arrives while the first request is still running. Because both try to insert the same primary key, PostgreSQL makes the second INSERT ... ON CONFLICT wait until the first transaction finishes. When the first commits, the second hits the conflict, does nothing, reads the saved response and replays it. If the first transaction fails and rolls back, the second one proceeds normally. No double charge, and no extra locking code.

A Real Gotcha: Calling an External Payment Provider

The example above works because the “work” is a database write. If your work calls an external provider, you should not hold a database transaction open during a slow network call. The usual approach is:

  1. Insert the key with a status of in_progress and commit.
  2. Call the provider, passing your own idempotency key along so it is also protected.
  3. Update the key with the final response and set the status to completed.
  4. If a retry arrives while the status is in_progress, return 409 Conflict (and tell the client to retry shortly).
  5. Run a recovery job for keys stuck in_progress for too long.

Don’t Forget the Client

The server is only half of the contract. A good client:
• Generates the key once per user action and reuses it for every retry of that action.
• Retries only when it makes sense: network errors, timeouts, 5xx and 429.
• Uses exponential backoff with jitter, so thousands of clients do not retry at the same instant.

Housekeeping

• Expire old keys. Keeping them forever grows the table. Many APIs keep them for a limited window (for example, 24 hours) and delete older ones with a scheduled job. Document the window for your clients.
• Decide what to store. Saving the outcome of every completed request keeps replays consistent. Let genuinely transient failures (a 503) be retried instead of cached.
• Index and size. The primary key is the only index you need for the lookup.

How to Say This in an Interview (45 Seconds)

“Retries after a timeout can double-charge a customer, because POST is not idempotent. I would require an Idempotency-Key header, a unique ID the client generates per action. On the server I store the key with a hash of the request and the saved response, with a unique constraint so concurrent attempts cannot both succeed. A repeat with the same key and body returns the saved response, the same key with a different body gets a 422, and a request still in progress gets a 409. I would expire keys after a window like 24 hours, and if I call an external provider, I would pass the key through to it.”

Common Mistakes

• Using GET or a database row count as a “double-click guard” instead of a real key.
• Generating a new key on each retry (which defeats the purpose).
• Not comparing the request body, so a reused key silently does the wrong thing.
• Holding a database transaction open while calling an external API.
• Forgetting to expire keys.

Keep Practising API Design

Idempotency is just one of the “hard parts” of API design interviews, alongside pagination, versioning, errors and rate limits. If you want to practise designing and defending APIs hands-on, the API Design Lab on ScaleDojo has 144 levels, and you can start for free.

articles.title: How Chrome DevTools Works Under the Hood
articles.description: A look under the hood of Chrome DevTools: its TypeScript frontend, 18-year history, and the Chrome DevTools Protocol.
articles.body_html:
This article is based on my talk "Chrome DevTools LIVE LIVE LIVE", presented at DevFest events in Modena, Málaga, Venezia, Vicenza, Birmingham, Dublin, and more.

As web developers, we spend hours debugging web applications using Chrome DevTools every week. But we rarely think about what's under the hood of Chrome DevTools. Unlike the rest of the browser, which is built using C++, Chrome DevTools is actually built using the technologies that we are very familiar with: HTML, CSS, and TypeScript.

In this article, we will look at how Chrome DevTools is built, how it evolved from a simple debugging tool 18 years ago to today's full debugging suite, as well as the protocol that powers Chrome DevTools itself.

Chrome DevTools Frontend

The Chrome DevTools UI (devtools-frontend) is an open-source web application built with TypeScript, HTML, CSS, Lit, and Web Components.

Back in 2013, the DevTools team was using Google's Closure Compiler and JSDoc annotations for type checking. However, as TypeScript got more popular over time, they decided to migrate the entire DevTools codebase to TypeScript. This took them over 13 months, but the result is that the codebase of DevTools looks very familiar to any frontend developer.

To run DevTools locally, you can follow the Chrome DevTools contribution guide. Fortunately, back in 2019, they detached DevTools itself from the massive Chromium monorepo. This means building and running DevTools locally doesn't require a powerful machine to build the entire Chromium C++ codebase.

Inspecting DevTools with DevTools

We use Chrome DevTools to debug the web applications we build. But since Chrome DevTools is also another web application, how do Googlers or DevTools contributors debug Chrome DevTools? The answer is that they use DevTools to debug DevTools!

Here's how to do it:

  1. Open Chrome DevTools by pressing F12, Cmd + Option + I on Mac, or Ctrl + Shift + I on Windows and Linux.
  2. Click the "Customize and control DevTools" (⋮) menu in the top-right corner and select the "Undock into separate window" icon next to Dock side.
  3. Click inside the undocked DevTools window to focus it, then press Cmd + Option + I (Mac) or Ctrl + Shift + I (Windows and Linux) a second time.

With this, you can now debug DevTools using another DevTools window. You can use the Elements panel to look at how the complex UI panels in DevTools are structured, or maybe run a performance audit on DevTools to see how well-optimized it is.

Or just for fun, you can repeat the process infinitely. You can use DevTools to debug another DevTools window, and then open a third DevTools window to debug the DevTools that is debugging the first DevTools, just like the movie Inception.

18 Years of DevTools Layout

Before 2006, developers often needed to use some weird, hacky workarounds to debug their websites. Then in 2006, Firebug was launched for Firefox as the first-of-its-kind devtools.

In 2008, Google launched the first version of Google Chrome. It bundled WebKit's Web Inspector directly into the browser itself.

Take note of the URL bar at the top of the window: chrome-resource://inspector/inspector.html. Even in Chrome 1.0, DevTools was already an HTML page running inside the browser.

Since the launch of the first version of DevTools 18 years ago, Chrome has added many new features and panels to it. However, if you compare Chrome 1.0 from 2008 with Chrome today, the core layout is still very similar:

  • Top Tabs (Elements and Resources): Elements is still the first tab today, while Resources later evolved into the Network, Application, and Sources panels.
  • DOM Tree and Breadcrumbs: The left pane shows the HTML tree, with the html > body > div breadcrumb bar at the bottom.
  • Styles Sidebar: The right pane already had Styles, Computed Style, Metrics, and Properties.
  • Console Drawer Toggle: The bottom-left corner has the same toggle buttons for docking and opening the Console drawer (>_).

The Chrome team got the core layout right from the beginning. Since 2008, most updates have expanded on this original layout instead of replacing it.

Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)

The Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) is a JSON-based protocol that connects debug and automation targets (such as browsing contexts and workers) with trusted debug and automation clients. It allows tools to instrument, inspect, debug, and profile Chromium, Chrome, and other Blink-based browsers.

CDP is used by Chrome, Chrome DevTools (including Chrome DevTools for Agents and Chrome DevTools MCP), Lighthouse, Puppeteer, and ChromeDriver.

Protocol Monitor

You can view the CDP messages sent between the Chrome browser and DevTools with the Protocol Monitor panel. It is an experimental panel that lets you view every CDP request and response sent between DevTools and the browser, and even send raw CDP commands yourself.

To enable the Protocol Monitor, you need to turn it on in DevTools Settings:

  1. Open Chrome DevTools and click the Settings gear icon in the top-right corner.
  2. In the Experiments tab, check "Protocol Monitor" and reload DevTools.
  3. Click the "Customize and control DevTools" (⋮) menu and select "More tools" > "Protocol Monitor".

Console Utilities API

When you evaluate expressions in the Console panel, DevTools uses CDP's Runtime.evaluate method with includeCommandLineAPI: true to inject the Console Utilities API, a collection of helper functions and shortcuts that dates all the way back to Firebug. Because CDP only injects these utilities when evaluating expressions from the Console, they are only available inside the Console panel and won't work inside your application's own JavaScript code.

For example, instead of typing document.querySelector() or document.querySelectorAll() in the Console panel, you can use $() or $$(). While these look just like jQuery, they actually originated in Firebug (inspired by Prototype.js) and were later adopted by WebKit's Web Inspector and Chrome DevTools.

Besides that, the Console Utilities API also provides shortcuts like $0 to $4. They return the last 5 DOM elements you selected in the Elements panel (or the last 5 heap objects selected in the Memory panel), where $0 is the currently selected element, $1 is the previous one, and so on.

Chrome DevTools Extensions

Chrome DevTools has over 30 panels, but it still can't cover every use case, especially when debugging web frameworks like React or Angular. With the chrome.devtools.* extension APIs, developers can create their own custom panels and sidebar panes in DevTools.

For example, React Developer Tools uses chrome.devtools.panels.create() to add the Components and Profiler tabs directly into DevTools. You can also build your own DevTools extension for your team to debug internal tools, feature flags, or state management.

However, DevTools is also making it easier for framework authors to visualize performance data without building a dedicated DevTools extension. In the past, to show a custom performance track, framework developers needed to use a DevTools extension to create a separate panel just to display their custom waterfall chart.

With the Performance extensibility API (built on console.timeStamp() and the User Timing API), they can now add custom tracks directly into the Performance panel without an extension API at all.

Conclusion

It is always fun to understand what's under the hood of the tool we use every day. Since Chrome DevTools is built with the same HTML, CSS, and TypeScript we already know, the next time you find a bug in DevTools, you know you actually have the superpower to fix it and benefit millions of web developers around the world.

articles.title: Passing a Room Key with 4 Pictures: Implementing SPAKE2 (RFC 9382) in the Browser
articles.description: Clipboard Share (https://www.clipboardapp.org), an online clipboard with no login, now has "rooms"....
articles.body_html:
Clipboard Share (https://www.clipboardapp.org), an online clipboard with no login, now has "rooms". Files and text you exchange in a room are encrypted on your device, file names included, and the room key is never sent to the server. The server only holds ciphertext.

Up to here, browser Web Crypto gets you there quickly. The hard part came next: how do you move the room key to a new device?

Three ways to move the key

  1. Same Wi-Fi: press "Connect in a room" on a device card. The key is wrapped with a one-time ECDH (P-256) key and handed over. Both screens must show the same 4 pictures, which you check by eye to block a man in the middle.
  2. QR code or invite link: the key goes after the # in the URL. Everything after # is not included in the request to the server. The app strips it from the address bar before any analytics script runs.
  3. Then there was the hard case: PC to PC, or phone to a PC with no camera. You can't scan a QR code, and nobody wants to retype a long link by hand.

So I copied the join code idea from Minecraft Education: a device already in the room shows 4 pictures, and the new device taps those 4 pictures, in order, out of 24. No memorizing, just look and tap.

4 pictures is too short for a password

Pick 4 out of 24 in order (repeats allowed) and you get 24⁴ = 331,776 possibilities. If you derived a key straight from that, anyone holding a single ciphertext could try all 330,000 in about a second.

Having the server ask "is this picture code right?" doesn't work either, because then the server learns the pictures, and could intercept the key handoff.

The properties I needed:

  • Only two devices that both know the short secret (4 pictures) end up with the same key.
  • Eavesdropping on the messages gives you nothing to brute-force offline.
  • An attacker can test only one guess per attempt.

That is a PAKE (Password-Authenticated Key Exchange). I picked SPAKE2 (RFC 9382), because the spec is short and standardized as an RFC.

SPAKE2 in a nutshell

On curve P-256, each side picks a random number, x and y. They mix the password w with public constant points M and N and send the result.

  • Joining side (A): pA = x·G + w·M
  • Room side (B): pB = y·G + w·N

The receiver subtracts the other side's blinding term w·M (or w·N) and multiplies by its own secret. If w matches, both land on K = x·y·G. If w differs even slightly, they get unrelated points, the confirmation MAC fails, and the exchange ends immediately. Someone who only sees pA and pB has no way to try candidate values of w one by one.

The implementation follows the RFC step by step on top of the P-256 point operations in @noble/curves (MIT). Hashing, HKDF and HMAC use browser Web Crypto. The module is loaded with a dynamic import only when a picture code is used, so it is not in the first-screen bundle.

// frontend/src/utils/spake2.js (excerpt)
const ownPoint = Point.BASE.multiply(mine).add(mulOrZero(myBlind, w))
...
const diff = peerPoint.subtract(mulOrZero(peerBlind, w))
if (diff.is0()) throw new Error('SPAKE2_BAD_POINT')
const K = diff.multiply(mine) // h = 1 (P-256 has cofactor 1)

A received point is rejected if it is not on the curve, if it is the identity, or if it becomes the identity after the subtraction. There are separate tests for this.

4 pictures → w 

// w = SHA-256("cs-code-v1" || 4 picture-index bytes || sessionId) mod n
export async function derivePassword(code, sessionId) { ... }

The RFC says to stretch the password with a slow hash (MHF). I deliberately didn't. This code can only be tried online: the server counts wrong attempts and blocks them, the code changes within 5 minutes, and every join attempt has a different sessionId, so nothing can be precomputed. Offline brute force is already ruled out by SPAKE2 itself.

The server only knows "which room"

The server has to find the room and connect the two devices, so it needs to be told something. Only the first 2 of the 4 pictures are sent (routeOf). The server uses them to find the room and relay messages, and it can't decrypt the contents.

// frontend/src/utils/pictureCode.js
export function routeOf(code) { return [code[0], code[1]] }

The first two pictures give only 24 × 24 = 576 combinations. So two codes open at the same time must not share the same first two. If they collide, the server returns ROUTE_TAKEN and the room-side device reopens with new pictures (up to 12 times). The server accepts at most 500 codes open at once.

Here is the cost of this design. Since the server knows the first two, a server that deliberately sat in the middle would have to guess the last two. That is 1 in 576 per attempt, and a wrong guess breaks the confirmation MAC, so the failed join becomes visible.

Four messages

Step Direction Content
A1 new device → room pA
B1 room → new device pB + room-side confirmation MAC
A2 new device → room new-device confirmation MAC
P room → new device {room key, entry ticket, room name} wrapped with AES-GCM

A successful key exchange doesn't let anyone in by itself. After A2 passes, the room-side screen shows "Sunny Otter wants to join" with [Decline] [Let in], and P is sent only after a person taps Let in. Even with the right pictures, a device the room's owner doesn't recognize can't get in.

Rate limiting has two layers. Each device gets a warning after 3 wrong tries and has to wait 3 minutes after 5. Each IP is limited to 30 wrong tries per 10 minutes. With many people behind one router, such as a school, one student's mistakes shouldn't lock out the whole class, so the per-IP limit is set separately and higher.

I matched the RFC test vectors first

The scariest state when writing crypto yourself is "it works, but it isn't the spec." So I put in the 4 sets of P-256 test vectors from RFC 9382 Appendix B as they are, and made the test pass first: pA, pB, K, TT, Ke, Ka, KcA, KcB and the confirmation MAC all have to match byte for byte.

it(`vector ${i + 1} (A='${v.idA}', B='${v.idB}'): pA, pB, K, TT, Hash(TT), Ke, Ka, KcA, KcB, confirmation MAC match`, ...)

Other tests:

  • 20 round trips with the same code always succeed, and changing even one picture always fails.
  • A different sessionId fails even with the same pictures.
  • Invalid points are rejected.

I built this feature with Claude Code. I checked the test vectors line by line against the RFC text myself.

What's still lacking

  • It's a web app. Browser-side encryption only holds if you trust the JavaScript the site serves you. That differs from end-to-end encryption in an installed app. The code is open source under MIT.
  • What the server sees. File size, upload time, the device name tag (animal, device, browser) and the IP address.
  • The default tabs are different. The default tabs, "Same network" and "Everyone", are encrypted only if you turn on "Lock with a password". Outside a room it is not automatic.
  • No way to remove a device. There is no feature yet to kick a device out of a room, which is why it asks once more before letting a device in.
  • Not enough real-device testing. I still need to test more on a real iPhone with Safari.

Try it at https://www.clipboardapp.org and I'd appreciate your feedback. You can also send it through "Send feedback" at the bottom of the site.

Originally published in Korean on velog.

articles.title: Juice 1.0 Is Here — Building UI Without Fighting Your Markup
articles.description: After years of development, experimentation, architectural decisions, and more CSS than I care to...
articles.body_html:
After years of development, experimentation, architectural decisions, and more CSS than I care to admit, Juice has officially reached v1.0.0.

And I couldn't be more excited to finally say that.

For those who haven't followed my previous articles, Juice is an open-source, attribute-first CSS and UI library I've been developing as part of CitrusWorx's WebEngine ecosystem.

It started with a relatively simple question:

What if building interfaces felt more like describing what you wanted, rather than constantly wrestling with how to style it?

That question eventually became Juice.

Today, I'm excited to share its first major release.

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Modern frontend development is incredibly powerful.

We have mature frameworks, sophisticated design systems, utility-first CSS libraries, component ecosystems, and tooling that would have seemed unimaginable a decade ago.

But somewhere along the way, building a relatively simple interface started requiring an increasingly complicated collection of abstractions.

Sometimes you need a component library.

Sometimes you need a CSS framework.

Sometimes you need a JavaScript framework just to make everything work together.

And sometimes, all you really want is a card with a heading, some content, and a button.

I kept asking myself whether we could make the everyday parts of UI development simpler without sacrificing the flexibility needed for more sophisticated applications.

I didn't want to reinvent CSS.

I wanted to rethink how we interact with it.

Enter Juice: Attribute-First UI Development

Juice takes a different approach to expressing layout and presentation.

Instead of relying entirely on lengthy class lists or custom component abstractions, Juice allows developers to describe their interfaces directly through HTML attributes.

For example, here's a conceptual illustration of the attribute-first approach:

<div stack gap="4">
  <div card padding="4">
    <h2>Welcome to Juice</h2>
    <p>
      Build interfaces with expressive markup.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>

The idea is straightforward:

Your markup describes the structure. Your theme defines the visual identity. Juice connects the two.

Attributes such as stack, row, grid, gap, padding, card, and surface make layout intentions visible where the interface is actually being constructed.

This isn't about replacing every CSS rule with an attribute.

It's about providing a more expressive foundation for the things developers do repeatedly.

More Than Another CSS Framework

One of the most important architectural decisions behind Juice was making it useful independently of WebEngine.

Although Juice is being developed as part of the larger CitrusWorx ecosystem, it isn't intended to require developers to adopt that entire ecosystem.

You should be able to use Juice in a standalone project, integrate it into an existing application, or combine it with the frontend technologies you already enjoy.

That independence matters to me.

I don't believe developers should have to replace their entire toolchain just to benefit from one useful library.

Juice is designed around a CSS-first foundation, with JavaScript capabilities available where they make sense.

Its broader architecture also brings together design tokens, themes, components, and optional runtime behavior.

The goal is to provide a consistent UI foundation without forcing every application into the same architecture.

Why Themes Matter

One of the principles driving Juice is the separation of structure and identity.

A layout shouldn't have to be completely rewritten just because an application needs a different visual personality.

The same structural building blocks should be reusable across projects while themes control how those building blocks look and feel.

For CitrusWorx, this is especially important.

WebEngine is intended to support a growing ecosystem of applications and developer tools.

Having a shared visual foundation means we can establish consistency without requiring every application to look identical.

That's the balance I'm working toward with Juice.

What v1.0.0 Actually Means

Reaching version 1.0 isn't the same as declaring a project finished.

If anything, it means accepting a new level of responsibility for the foundation you've created.

During the 0.x development cycle, I spent a considerable amount of time exploring the boundaries of what Juice should become.

There were questions about how attributes should behave, how themes should work, how much JavaScript belongs in a CSS-first library, and how to organize the different pieces into something developers can reasonably understand.

There was also the temptation to keep adding features.

Another component.

Another runtime.

Another abstraction.

Another improvement before calling it ready.

Eventually, though, a library needs to stop being an endless experiment and start becoming something people can actually build with.

Juice v1.0.0 represents that transition.

It's a commitment to a public foundation that developers can begin adopting, testing, and helping improve.

It doesn't mean every idea on the roadmap has been implemented.

It means the project has reached its first major milestone, and future improvements can build on that foundation.

Juice and the Bigger WebEngine Picture

If you've followed my Road to WebEngine series, you know Juice isn't being developed in isolation.

It's one part of a much larger effort at CitrusWorx to build an ecosystem of modular, interoperable developer technologies.

Another major part of that ecosystem is Sig.js, our JavaScript library for building reactive interfaces.

With Sig.js and Juice both reaching their first major releases, two important pieces of the WebEngine vision are beginning to come together.

Sig.js addresses how interfaces are constructed and updated.

Juice addresses how those interfaces are structured and presented.

They have different responsibilities, and that's intentional.

I want developers to be able to adopt individual pieces of WebEngine without being forced into an all-or-nothing framework decision.

The broader vision is ambitious, but it's being built one library, one package, and one release at a time.

Getting Started

Juice v1.0.0 is available on npm.

npm install @citrusworx/juiceui@1.0.0

You can explore the package and source code here:

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@citrusworx/juiceui/v/1.0.0

GitHub: https://github.com/citrusworx/webengine/tree/master/libraries/juice

Whether you're interested in attribute-driven styling, design systems, frontend architecture, or simply exploring a different approach to building interfaces, I'd love for you to take a look.

What's Next?

Reaching v1.0.0 doesn't mean development slows down.

It means the focus changes.

Moving forward, I want to spend more time improving the developer experience, refining documentation, expanding practical examples, addressing issues that emerge from real-world usage, and continuing to evolve the library without losing sight of its original purpose.

I also want to explore how Juice can make UI development more accessible to people who aren't necessarily frontend specialists.

Because I believe good developer tools should make creativity easier, not introduce unnecessary barriers.

A Personal Milestone

Building something like Juice takes a surprising amount of persistence.

There are days when everything comes together beautifully.

And there are days when you find yourself questioning an architectural decision you made three months earlier.

But that's part of engineering.

You experiment.

You discover limitations.

You rethink assumptions.

You improve the design.

And eventually, you ship.

For me, Juice reaching v1.0.0 is another step toward turning CitrusWorx from a collection of ideas and experiments into a real ecosystem of software that other developers can use.

There's still an enormous amount of work ahead.

But today, I'm celebrating this milestone.

Juice 1.0 is here.

If you try it, I'd genuinely appreciate your feedback. Tell me what works, what doesn't, and what you think an attribute-first UI library should do differently.

Thanks for following along on the Road to WebEngine.

We're just getting started.

Built with curiosity, persistence, and a whole lot of CSS.

#webdev #css #opensource #javascript
