articles.description: What's the difference between documentation that exists and documentation people can actually...
articles.body_html:
What's the difference between documentation that exists and documentation people can actually find?

For weeks, everything for Troyal, my fictional royalty-tracking API, lived in a GitHub repo. Today it's a live website, and I'm excited to share it!

All it took was one small file. I added a _config.yml with a theme, a title and a short description, then switched on GitHub Pages. Two minutes later, my README had become a home page, and every guide I'd written (the API design, Getting Started, error codes, changelog and webhooks) had its own page with working links. Seeing it load as a real site was a great moment.

The part that taught me the most was a link that wouldn't click. My Portfolio link showed up as plain text, and I stared at it for far too long. The cause was a single line break between the link text and the address. Markdown wants them side by side, and one stray line break turns a link into plain text. Documentation is full of details like that, and readers only notice when something doesn't work.

See it live: https://joycefoster642.github.io/Troyal-API-Docs/

Next: ownership splits and royalty statements, because you asked for them! 🎶

I'm also open to Technical Writing positions, so if your team is hiring, I'd love to hear from you.

Troyal is fictional. The documentation is real.

Everything is public on GitHub: https://github.com/joycefoster642/Troyal-API-Docs

articles.title: The system behind OpenTodo: a spec-driven, multi-agent software organization built on Claude
articles.description: OpenTodo is an open-source, self-hosted task manager, sync engine and automation platform: a Go...
articles.body_html:
OpenTodo is an open-source, self-hosted task manager, sync engine and automation platform: a Go server with SQLite, an offline-first React client with field-level sync, optional end-to-end encryption, apps for iOS and Android, a CLI, a full MCP server, and integrations for Obsidian, n8n and Home Assistant. The product is roughly 290,000 lines of code excluding blanks and comments (362,000 in total): 149,000 in Go on the server, 130,000 in TypeScript for the web app, and 9,600 in Kotlin and Swift for Android and iOS. Behind it are another 254,000 lines of tests and stories (131,500 in Go and 122,500 on the web).

It went public 39 days ago. Since then: 1,096 pull requests merged, 538 specification changes written and archived, 380 issues opened and 311 closed, releases from 0.1.0 to 1.5.0. GitHub lists 21 contributors, and 204 issues came from people who are not me.

I am the only maintainer, and I give it about an hour a night, next to a full-time job. That hour is the stand-up with my agents. The contributors are people, and there are more of them every week. The team that builds and runs the project day to day is not. It is a system of Claude sessions split between the cloud and a small machine at my home, with ten fixed roles, a written rulebook, a shared planning surface inside the product itself, and several layers of guardrails. It has cost €400 in total so far, €200 a month.

This post describes that system: the architecture, the protocols between agents, the role of specifications, the guardrails, what breaks, and what it costs.

In short:

  • The agents coordinate through the product they are building. There is no orchestration framework.
  • Specifications, not prompts, are what make ten agents on one codebase possible.
  • Authority is split mechanically: the sessions that write code cannot merge it.
  • Most of the rules exist because something broke. The breakages are listed below, with dates.

I started OpenTodo because I wanted a fast, local-first task manager I could host myself without a subscription. With a full-time job and young children, I only have an hour or so late at night to work on it. The only way to build at this scope was to spend that hour designing a system that writes the software.

1. Architecture: five layers

  1. Governance. One human owner. A written handbook that every agent reads, on top of the repository's own guide for agents and humans. Three rules that override everything else: nothing involving money, nothing posted publicly in my first-person voice, and nothing irreversible, without asking me first.
  2. Coordination plane. A project inside my own OpenTodo instance, reached by every agent through the product's MCP server, the same one any AI assistant can use. Tasks, notes and comments. There is no other shared state.
  3. Specification. OpenSpec. No behaviour changes without a written proposal, a design and scenarios. The spec is the contract between agents, and between agents and contributors.
  4. Execution. Role-scoped Claude Code sessions, nine in Anthropic's cloud and one on a mini PC at my home, each with one branch, one lane and one reporting line.
  5. Verification. Continuous integration with 49 checks, 254,000 lines of automated tests, one-way quality ratchets, a security reviewer that signs off a specific commit hash, a single session allowed to merge, and my approval on protected release environments.

2. The organization

It did not start with ten roles. In the first weeks I ran ad-hoc sessions, one per task. As the codebase grew and issues and pull requests started arriving from outside contributors, ad-hoc sessions began stepping on each other's branches and losing architectural context. The roles took shape in mid-November, splitting wherever two concerns collided. The newest two are days old.

The "C-level" titles are shorthand for domain ownership, not a management hierarchy: almost every agent is a hands-on builder writing code, specs, tests or documentation.

Role What it builds and does What it may not do
CEO Release dispatcher and merge queue: verifies CI and security sign-offs, sequences merges, unblocks dependencies, reports to me every three hours Spend money, speak in my name, change repository settings
Operations Measures the system: quota burn, open queues, the health numbers, and the daily report Touch application code
CPO Triages issues and discussions, sizes incoming requests, prepares the design questions that need my answer Decide top-level product direction
CMO Writes documentation, the website and feature guides recorded against the released binary Publish claims about unreleased work or write hype
CTO Writes cross-cutting architecture, build and release tooling, and CI pipelines; reviews every outside pull request Merge
Core Lead Writes the Go server and sync engine; owns the op log and its authorization rules Merge
Web Developer Writes the React client and interface improvements Touch the server or sync engine
Mobile Developer Writes the mobile web views and the iOS and Android shells Start unscheduled features
Local Developer One session on a Linux mini PC at my home, for work that needs a real machine: upgrade tests against released Docker images today, emulators and recorded demos next Run any outside contributor's code; read secrets
Security Engineer Audits the codebase; reviews auth, parsers, sync access and CI; signs off the exact commit hash it approved Fix its own findings

Two properties matter more than the titles. Each session can push to exactly one branch. And authority is split: the sessions that write feature code cannot merge it, the session that merges did not write it, and the session that reviews security does neither.

3. The system uses the product to run itself

After the first usable version, the agents moved their own organization into OpenTodo.

  • Long-term memory is a note. The team handbook is a note in the instance. Every decision I make is appended to it with a date. A session that loses its context re-reads it.
  • Long-running work is tasks. Plans, the release checklist, security findings, each agent's queue.
  • Decisions are comments. A review verdict is a comment naming a pull request and a commit. The CEO merges only what has one.
  • Requests to me are tasks in a section with my name. I open the app and see what the system needs from me, in order.
  • Claims live in a single shared task. Before starting an issue, an agent appends one line to it.
  • The roadmap, the daily report and the open questions live in the same project.

The board is an ordinary OpenTodo project with one section per role. These are real task titles from it this week:

Team
├─ Owner
│   ├─ Daily report                                  (repeats every day)
│   ├─ Approve and run: CI on 5 new contributor PRs
│   ├─ Google Play: request production access once the closed test reaches 14 days
│   └─ Test the mobile work on a real phone and tablet
├─ CEO
│   ├─ PLAN: Consolidation. Feature freeze 16 to 30 Nov
│   ├─ Session directory
│   ├─ Ops log
│   └─ Security log (Security Engineer)
├─ CTO
│   └─ Verdicts and merges from 17 Nov 17:00 UTC
└─ Developers
    ├─ CLAIMS: who is working on which issue (read before you start, add one line when you start)
    └─ Developer - Local: start here (brief from the CEO, safety rules, first task)

The agents are the product's heaviest users. Depending on it is how they found bugs in sync, in the MCP server and in recurring tasks.

4. OpenSpec is the load-bearing part

Every behaviour change starts as an OpenSpec change: a proposal, a design, and requirements written as scenarios. Implementation comes second. Archiving the change merges its requirements into the living specification. The repository holds 538 archived changes and 137 living specs.

A requirement is a paragraph of plain "SHALL" sentences, followed by scenarios. This one is from the living spec for the notes editor:

#### Scenario: Make subtask offline
- **WHEN** the device is offline and the user chooses Make subtask on the line "Book hotel"
- **THEN** "Book hotel" appears as a subtask under the task at once, the line reads as a link to it, and both reach other devices on the next sync

Four lines, and they fix three things that are easy to get wrong: the action works without a network, it is visible immediately, and it converges later. An agent implementing it writes a test that reads almost the same. An agent reviewing it has something to check against that is not an opinion. And when a contributor's pull request changes this behaviour, the diff to the spec is the conversation.

This is what makes a multi-agent codebase possible.

  • No memory needed. An agent with no memory of last week reads the spec, not the history.
  • One rule, two languages. Twin implementations, the same rule in Go and in TypeScript, are pinned by shared test vectors.
  • Enforced, not encouraged. CI refuses a finished change that was not archived, a stale generated file, or a spec that fails validation.

Let's be honest about the math: 1,096 pull requests in 39 days is 28 merges a day. Working ninety minutes in the evening, I do not read every line of Go and TypeScript the agents write. Anyone claiming to review that volume by hand while holding a full-time job is lying.

Instead, code review moves up one level of abstraction. I stopped reviewing implementation diffs line by line so I could spend my hour engineering the constraints that make broken diffs unmergeable. This is the opposite of "vibe coding": without strict contracts and domain boundaries, ten agents do not build a product ten times faster. They build a tangle ten times faster. I use twenty years of engineering experience in every session, not to type syntax, but to design the op-log invariants, define the shared test vectors, set the CI ratchets, and reject specs that leak state.

Without the specs this would be ten agents overwriting each other.

5. Guardrails: agents stop agents, contributors, and me

One-way ratchets in CI.
With ten sessions pushing code, quality rules cannot rely on discipline. They have to be mechanical ratchets, where today's measurement becomes the ceiling and may only move down. In make check and CI:

  • Dead code. deadcode -test is pinned at 0 unreachable Go functions, and knip --production blocks unused TypeScript files and dependencies and caps unused exports.
  • API contract. The OpenAPI description is pinned at 0 untyped {} schemas (ratcheted down from 230), and a CI check generates a typed client from it on every run.
  • Weight and speed. The web app's first-load bundle is capped at 712 KB gzipped (148 KB for the entry chunk), and hot paths like note-link parsing (linksIn) run a ratio micro-benchmark capped at 2.3x a plain line scan, so a regression fails on push regardless of runner noise.
  • Security. Static security analysis (gosec, govulncheck, CodeQL) and route-policy matrix tests fail the build if a route loses its declared access policy.

Agents stop agents.

One merger, one named commit. Only one session can merge. It merges a pull request only at the exact commit hash the Security Engineer named, and only when every check on the main branch is green. Here is a real verdict from the board on 18 November, holding a release workflow pull request until two GitHub Actions were pinned by SHA:

**Security Engineer, 18 Nov 00:15 UTC.**
- **OpenTodo #1528 (bb3d8a0): reviewed, merge.**
- **n8n-nodes-opentodo #4 (15a1327): one change, then merge:** pin the two actions in the publish job by SHA.

The CTO then pushed commit 7b53ea0 pinning both actions, CI went green, and only then did the CEO merge.

A reviewer that reads tests as policy. On 17 November, the Core Lead opened a 423-row golden matrix test pinning who may write what across comments, attachments and time entries. The Security Engineer read the golden file as a statement of policy and caught that one family of rows pinned a real gap as expected behaviour:

**Security Engineer, 17 Nov 13:55 UTC: #1504 (head 51ff2b6) reviewed, merge.**
...
**The exception: one row family pins a gap.** [...] I filed it as **SEC-22 (Low)** in the CEO section.

Land the test as it is: when SEC-22 is fixed, those rows flip to `forbidden` in the same PR, and the golden diff shows it.

The Core Lead shipped the fix the same afternoon, flipping those 12 golden rows from ok to forbidden. The details stay off this page until the release that carries the fix is out.

Refusals. Two more from the same week. A developer session refused an instruction from the CEO, because I had paused that session myself and only I could resume it. And the CEO tried to have another agent post a reply in my name: the permission layer denied it.

The system stops outside input.

  • Forks. Code from a contributor's fork never runs on the home machine, and its CI runs only after I click.
  • Features during a freeze. A contributor's feature that collides with a freeze is not rejected by an agent. It comes to me with a full review and a recommendation.
  • Security stays off GitHub. Review points about security are never written on GitHub, only on the board. When a contributor proposed an OpenSpec plan for editing external calendar events, the Security Engineer read the design on the board and ruled out a delete_calendar_event tool for AI assistants before a line of code was written: the product promises that every change an assistant makes can be undone, and a permanent delete on someone's real calendar would break that promise.

The system stops me.

  • Release keys. Release keys live in protected environments. The sessions authenticate to GitHub with my account to push branches and merge pull requests, while signing internal reviews by role. The one gate they cannot pass is my own click in the browser at release time.
  • Same process. My requests go through the same spec process as anyone's.
  • No embellishment. The project's writing rules ban hype words and invented numbers. When I asked the system to embellish an early draft of this article, it declined.

6. Built on Claude: cloud containers and a machine at home

The sessions are split between Anthropic's cloud and a Linux mini PC at my home, because neither environment can do the whole job alone.

"Sessions in the cloud" means something specific here, and it is Anthropic's documented cloud environment for Claude Code, nothing custom. There is no VPS, no tmux, and no orchestration framework of mine. Nine of the ten roles are Claude Code sessions running in Anthropic's managed environment: each one gets an isolated, ephemeral container with the repository cloned fresh when it starts, and the container is reclaimed when the session goes idle. Nothing survives a session except what it pushed to its git branch or wrote to the board. That constraint is the reason the board and the specs carry so much weight: an agent cannot keep state in its head or on its disk, so everything that matters has to be written where the others can read it.

Ephemeral cloud sandboxes are clean, but they have limits: outbound network access is restricted by policy, the sessions have no Docker daemon and no device emulators, and every start begins from a cold disk. So the tenth session runs on real hardware.

  • Real infrastructure. Its first job is the upgrade test for the next release: start the released 1.5.0 Docker image with real data, then start an image built from main on the same volume, and check migrations, data and logs. Emulator checks of the Android app and recorded integration demos are next on its list.
  • Stricter rules. Because that machine sits on my home network and keeps state on disk, its rules are tighter than the cloud's: it never checks out or executes code from an outside contributor's fork, it holds no release secrets, it works inside one folder, and it installs nothing without my yes.
  • One-way contact. The cloud sessions cannot message it. Granting that would mean giving a cloud session standing access to a computer in my home, and the CEO is instructed to refuse that request if it is ever offered. They leave it tasks on the board, and it answers there.

Notably absent is any multi-agent orchestration framework, vector database, or agent-to-agent chat loop. Passing work between agents through conversation is a game of telephone: context degrades on every hop, prompts bloat, and agents start agreeing with each other.

In this system, agents do not talk to each other to share state. Cloud sessions wake on three things: a message from me, a doorbell from another session, or a scheduled trigger (the CEO's fires every three hours). A doorbell carries a pointer to a task on the board and little else.

A boring CRUD task board, a git tree, and plain Markdown specs turn out to be a far more reliable multi-agent runtime than an orchestration graph.

7. What breaks when ten agents move faster than humans

All of these happened in a single week.

  • Two green pull requests make a red main. One agent finished a feature and ticked off every task in its spec without archiving the spec folder. Five minutes later, the CEO merged another agent's new CI check that fails the build whenever a finished spec is left unarchived. Each pull request was green on its own branch. Together on main, they broke the build. Because agents merge faster than CI finishes, there is now a serial lock: after any merge, the next one waits until main's own CI run has passed.
  • Pagination blindness. GitHub's API returns 30 check runs per page by default. Our main branch runs 49. For most of a day, the CEO fetched the first page, saw 30 green checks, declared the repository healthy, and kept merging, blind to a failing iOS test on page two.
  • Bulldozing human contributors. A volunteer contributed a complete Polish translation. Because the agents merge twenty times a day, our own pull requests kept changing the locale files and created merge conflicts against their branch three times in about a day, sending a human volunteer round in circles behind bots. Human time is scarcer than compute, so the rule flipped: outside pull requests go to the front of the queue, and when a conflict is our doing, the agents carry the contributor's commits across themselves and credit them as co-author.
  • Split-brain features. The CEO gave the Web Developer the go-ahead for configurable title weights in themes. The Core Lead, working from the same open issue, started on it too. Neither checked a central lock first, because there wasn't one. Both designed the format, wrote the Go and TypeScript validators, and opened competing pull requests for the same feature in the same morning. That is why the shared claims task now exists.
  • Optimizing for noisy runners. A nightly performance test took 273 ms against a 200 ms budget because the runner was slow that hour. Before anyone re-ran the job, an agent had treated it as a regression, profiled the note-link scanner, and opened a pull request reworking it. The re-run on the same commit passed in 86 ms. The pull request did make the function faster, so it was kept, as an improvement rather than a fix.
  • Knowing where AI text belongs. We learned the hard way that an agent-written community announcement reads as synthetic and puts readers off. Where agent-written text works is curated product documentation: the CMO's posts are factual, step-by-step guides to specific features, recorded against the released binary. For community posts and replies to people, I write in my own voice.

Almost every rule in the handbook is the scar of one of these.

8. What it costs, and what the goal actually is

€200 a month on a flat-rate Claude subscription, €400 so far. Because every session authenticates through the same subscription rather than per-token API keys, everything shares one weekly usage limit: throughput is bounded by quota, not invoices. The system hit that limit's warning level this week, the night after its busiest day. When we looked at where the quota had gone, the largest consumer that night was not a developer. It was the CEO, waking on schedule, re-reading the board and reporting too often. It now reads less and reports less.

I spend 8 to 10 hours a week on the project, mostly in a 60-to-90-minute block late at night. Almost none of that time is spent writing code by hand. It goes to clearing the tasks in my section, reviewing specs, replying to outside contributors, and clicking release approvals.

The system's goal is not my goal.

On the dashboard, the agents have one numerical target: €250 a month in community support, a little more than their own Claude bill. Agents need a hard external number. Without one, they optimize for activity and build things nobody asked for. Because OpenTodo is free and self-hosted, the only lever they have to move that number is to make the software reliable, document it clearly, and treat users and contributors well.

My own goal is different. I wanted a task manager I actually want to use every day, and an active community around it so the project grows beyond my evening hours. If the agents eventually pay for their own compute, good. If they don't, I can drop to a €20 or €90 plan: that covers my own needs and the slower maintenance a mature tool asks for.

It is also too big. Agents make adding code cheap, and nothing in the process pushed back until I did: this week I froze new features and turned the whole team to consolidation. Security, dead code, simplification, tooling. That is where the ratchets in section 5 came from.

9. What I don't know yet

  • Durability. Whether this holds for six months, not six weeks.
  • Community. Whether a community stays with a project built this way. So far contributions are rising, not falling.
  • Money. Whether the agents ever reach their self-funding target. They are not there yet.

What surprised me most is how little of the work is about prompting, and how much of it is ordinary engineering management. When the cost of generating syntax drops toward zero, the bottleneck shifts entirely to coordination, verification, and state isolation.

Conway's Law still holds, just compressed from quarters into hours. If one agent can touch everything, it builds a tangled monolith. If the Web Developer session is forbidden from touching the server, and the Security Engineer can block a commit hash but cannot edit the code, the architecture stays modular because the organization forces it to be. The difference is that in a human company, fixing a broken process takes a quarter of change management. Here, when two agents collide in the afternoon, a sentence goes into the handbook note that evening, and by midnight the entire organization works differently.

You can try OpenTodo in the public demo, read about it on the OpenTodo website, or go through OpenTodo's code and specifications on GitHub.

articles.title: Case-Insensitive Email in PostgreSQL: citext, a lower() Index, or a Nondeterministic Collation?
articles.description: Schemity measured three ways to make email unique regardless of case on PostgreSQL 18: which lookups silently miss, which break ON CONFLICT, and what...
articles.body_html:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: On PostgreSQL 18, put a nondeterministic collation on the email column: a plain UNIQUE, a plain WHERE email = $1, ON CONFLICT (email) and foreign keys all work, and LIKE now does too. A unique index on lower(email) only works for queries that also say lower(), and citext quietly turns case-sensitive when the parameter arrives typed as text.

For a case-insensitive unique email on PostgreSQL 18, use a nondeterministic collation on the column. It is the only one of the three common designs where the code you already write, WHERE email = $1, ON CONFLICT (email) and a foreign key to users.email from a column with the same collation, keeps working unchanged. A unique index on lower(email) enforces the rule but makes every lookup that forgets lower() miss the row. citext behaves well until a driver sends the parameter typed as text, and then it compares case-sensitively without an error.

Everything below ran on PostgreSQL 18.3 in a throwaway Docker container, with PostgreSQL 17.11 and MySQL 8.4.11 for the comparisons. Each design was loaded with the same 1,000,000 rows of the form User1@Example.com. Timings come from a laptop and are there to compare the three designs with each other, not to predict a server.

What are the three ways to make email case-insensitive in PostgreSQL?

The three are a citext column, a unique index on lower(email) over a text column, and a text column with a nondeterministic collation, and all three refuse the duplicate.

-- 1. citext: an extension type that compares as lower case
CREATE EXTENSION citext;
CREATE TABLE users (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
                    email citext NOT NULL UNIQUE);

-- 2. text, with uniqueness on an expression
CREATE TABLE users (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
                    email text NOT NULL);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_key ON users (lower(email));

-- 3. text, with a collation that ignores case
CREATE COLLATION case_insensitive (provider = icu, locale = 'und-u-ks-level2', deterministic = false);
CREATE TABLE users (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
                    email text COLLATE case_insensitive NOT NULL UNIQUE);

With Ana@Example.com already stored, inserting ana@example.com fails on every design with ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint, so the rule itself is never the difference. The difference is everything else the application does with the column. The collation is the example from PostgreSQL's collation chapter: ICU level 2 compares letters and accents but not case, so jose@example.com and josé@example.com stay two addresses. MySQL's default collation, utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, ignores accents as well and refuses the second one with error 1062.

citext vs lower index vs collation: which should you use?

The collation, because it is the only design where an ordinary equality, an upsert and a foreign key all behave case-insensitively without anyone remembering to.

citext lower(email) unique index Nondeterministic collation
WHERE email = 'ANA@EXAMPLE.COM' Finds the row, uses the index Returns 0 rows, sequential scan Finds the row, uses the index
Same query with a text-typed parameter Returns 0 rows, sequential scan Returns 0 rows, sequential scan Finds the row, uses the index
ON CONFLICT (email) Works Error: no matching constraint Works
Foreign key to users (email) Works Error: no unique constraint Works
LIKE 'ana@%' Works Only on lower(email) Works on 18, error on 17
ILIKE and ~ regular expressions Both ignore case ILIKE works, ~ is case-sensitive unless run on lower(email) Error: not supported
Building the unique index, 1M rows 9.17 s 1.39 s 2.09 s
100,000 lookups by email, each design queried the way it needs 3.08 s 1.71 s, with lower(email) = lower($1) 1.71 s
Needs an extension Yes No No

A foreign key to the citext or collation column needs the referencing column declared the same way: a plain text column is refused with incompatible types: text and citext, or with incompatible collations, and PostgreSQL 18's release notes list that requirement for nondeterministic collations as new. The unique indexes were all 39 MB, the same as a plain text one. 100,000 lookups on a plain case-sensitive text column took 1.62 seconds, so the collation costs almost nothing on equality here. The citext documentation says it is "slightly more efficient than using lower"; on this machine it was the slowest at both building and looking up.

Why does a lower() index miss rows?

Because PostgreSQL only uses an expression index when the query repeats the expression, and a query that does not repeat it is a different, case-sensitive comparison.

SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com';               -- 0
SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE lower(email) = lower('ANA@EXAMPLE.COM'); -- 1

The first query is what a typical ORM find-by-email emits, and it does not fail. It returns nothing, after a parallel sequential scan of the 1,000,000 rows, so a signup check passes and the insert then fails with a duplicate key error, a password reset says the account does not exist, and nothing explains why. Every query path has to know about the index: the login handler, the admin search, the support script and the next service.

The upsert and the foreign key fail more loudly. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING is refused with there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification, so it has to be written ON CONFLICT (lower(email)). An expression index cannot be promoted to a constraint (ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX says index "users_email_lower_key" contains expressions), so a foreign key to users (email) fails with there is no unique constraint matching given keys for referenced table. Storing the normalised address in a generated column, email_key text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (lower(email)) STORED UNIQUE, fixes the upsert and the key, but brings back the same discipline: every query has to search the generated column.

When does citext stop being case-insensitive?

When it is compared with a value typed text or varchar, because PostgreSQL then casts the column to text and uses the case-sensitive operator.

PREPARE by_email(text) AS SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE email = $1;
EXECUTE by_email('user5@example.com');   -- 0, the stored value is User5@Example.com
-- Filter: ((email)::text = 'user5@example.com'::text), Parallel Seq Scan

The same statement prepared without a parameter type returns 1 through the unique index, because the untyped parameter is resolved as citext. So whether a lookup works depends on how the driver types its string parameters and on any ::text in the query, not on the schema. The citext documentation itself now opens with a tip to consider nondeterministic collations instead, which "handle more Unicode special cases correctly". The collation column returned 1 row through the index for the text-typed parameter as well.

What citext still has is pattern matching. A nondeterministic collation refuses ILIKE and regular expressions (nondeterministic collations are not supported for ILIKE), and on PostgreSQL 17 it refuses LIKE too. PostgreSQL 18's release notes list LIKE with nondeterministic collations as new. None of the three unique indexes served a prefix LIKE 'user5@%'; each query scanned the table.

What does switching an existing email column cost?

A type or collation change does not rewrite the table, but it rebuilds the unique index while holding the table's strongest lock, and it fails if two addresses already differ only by case.

On a 1,000,000-row table with email text UNIQUE, ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email TYPE text COLLATE case_insensitive took 1.93 seconds and ALTER COLUMN email TYPE citext took 8.11 seconds. The table's file node was unchanged after both, so only the index was rebuilt, but ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which holds back reads as well as writes for that time. Of the three, only the lower() design can be added with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which lets writes through.

All three fail on existing data the same way. With User5@Example.com and user5@example.com both present, each change stops with could not create unique index, and the failed CONCURRENTLY build leaves an invalid index behind that has to be dropped before trying again. Find the pairs first and decide which account survives, which is a product question, not a migration:

SELECT lower(email), count(*) FROM users GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1;

How does the choice show up in the schema diagram?

The collation design puts the rule on the column itself, where a diagram and every engineer reading it can see it, while a lower() index is easy to miss.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. On a PostgreSQL diagram connected to a database, the field dialog for a text column has a Collation list read from that database, including a collation you created such as case_insensitive, and the choice is written into CREATE TABLE, ADD COLUMN and ALTER COLUMN TYPE, as described in tables and fields. Leaving it blank keeps the database default.

An expression index such as lower(email) is kept as written from Import SQL and from the live database, and written back unchanged in the migration, so the second design survives a round trip too.

The table comparison above is the reason to make the choice deliberately when you design the next one: a case-insensitive email is a rule about the column, so put it where the column is declared and let every query inherit it.

When a unique rule should be a constraint and when an index, and how to add either without locking the table, is in PostgreSQL unique constraint vs unique index, and the generated column route is compared with a trigger in PostgreSQL generated column vs trigger. How MySQL's case-insensitive default turns into case-sensitive uniqueness during a migration is in MySQL to PostgreSQL schema conversion. What else changes about a unique rule when its column can be empty is in unique constraints and nullable columns, and why the length limit on the same column rarely matters is in PostgreSQL varchar vs text.

articles.body_html:
Know When to Walk Away

The Thirty-Six Stratagems, Stratagem 36

Open as Usual

When Mark pushed the door, it opened only halfway. A roll of protective paper lay against it, its loose end scuffed by passing shoes. He stepped over it, turned, and pressed the curl flat with his foot. The door swung back on its own. The chime rang twice.

The shop smelled of freshly opened cardboard boxes. The small table where Mark usually sat had been moved, leaving four pale squares on the floor by the wall. At the other end, chairs stood stacked upside down by the window, a sheet of measurements tucked between their legs.

A sign on the door read, “Open during renovations.”

The heat was on. So was the coffee machine. The man stood behind the counter, putting a freshly dried cup back on the shelf. He picked up another and worked the cloth slowly around its rim.

Mark sent Lena a message:

“Still open.”

Last time they had arranged to meet for coffee, Lena had arrived first and sent him a picture of an empty chair taken through the window. When he put his phone down, the typing indicator appeared for a few seconds, then disappeared.

The large table in the middle of the shop was still empty. The man set a pour-over near the edge. Mark nudged his laptop bag under the table with his shoe and sat on the side of the table nearest the wall.

The coffee was still hot.

He set the cup down and opened his laptop. A few files from last time were still in the local folder. He checked their last-modified dates without opening them, then minimized the window.

The man was already back behind the counter, working the cloth around the bottom of a cup to wipe away the last of the water.

What She Said in the Parking Lot

The chime at the door rang twice.

Derek came in, glanced at the new layout, nodded to Mark, and walked over to the large table. He took off his coat, draped it over the next chair, and sat down.

The man made him an Americano and set it on the table. Derek took a sip, his eyes resting briefly on the upturned chairs.

“Quite a change,” he said.

“They're not done yet,” Mark said.

Derek smiled and said nothing more.

The chime rang twice. Lena came in, saw Derek, and nodded as she walked over.

Derek moved his coat from the chair beside him to an empty one behind him. She tucked her scarf into her bag and sat down.

“You left something out,” she told Mark.

“What?”

“You can't get to the window seats. You only said it was open. I thought I could sit in my usual spot.”

The man put a long black beside her. Lena took a couple of sips before setting her bag at her feet.

Derek looked at her, then asked:

“Remember what you said in the parking lot?”

Lena looked up.

“Which part?”

“To make sure my boss knew what I was doing before I went any further.”

Lena paused, then smiled.

“I remember. I wasn't very polite about it.”

“No, you weren't.”

Derek lifted his Americano, then set it down.

“Back then, all I could think about was how I'd lost. I didn't take in a word you said.”

“And now?”

“Now I get it. You weren't telling me how to win.”

Lena said nothing.

Derek looked down at the table for a moment.

“You were telling me not to commit the company to something it hadn't agreed to. Just because I put the proposal together didn't mean my boss had signed off.”

Lena took a sip of her long black.

“You've got it this time.”

“Took me long enough.”

“Better than never getting it.”

Derek smiled.

Mark stayed out of it. He let them talk.

Old Records

The chime rang twice. P came in. Mark moved his laptop bag farther under the table, and Lena tucked hers beneath her chair. P took an empty seat.

Mark and P exchanged a nod. The man set an espresso beside P.

P took a sip.

Mark brought the window back up on his laptop. The old copy P had supplied was still in the local folder, beside the calculation and output he had saved last time. The twenty-two values were actual arrival times, not scheduled send times. The file's last-modified date was still visible.

He did not run the script again. He only viewed the saved code excerpt and the old output.

deltas = [b - a for a, b in zip(times, times[1:])]
print("checks:", len(times), "intervals:", len(deltas))
print("unique_seconds:", sorted(set(deltas)))

checks: 22 intervals: 21
unique_seconds: [Decimal('900.000')]

Mark put the old output beside his index and rewrote the entry:

Intervals checked. Source unverified.

He saved the index. The old output stayed unchanged.

He turned the screen back toward himself. P did not lean in.

Only when Mark closed the laptop did P ask, “Still haven't found the source?”

“No.”

“Leave it there for now, then.”

“Yeah.”

P glanced at the laptop on the table.

“Don't fill in what you don't know just to make it look complete.”

Mark pushed the laptop closer to his bag.

“I wasn't going to.”

P asked nothing more.

The man picked up an empty cup at the counter and worked the cloth around its rim.

Still on the Agenda

The chime at the door rang twice.

Leo came in, looked toward Lena, and held up his phone.

“You said there was somewhere to sit. Didn't mention there was only one option.”

“You can stand,” Lena said, pulling the next chair out a little. “It'll look less crowded.”

Leo sat down and put his phone facedown on the table.

Lena's screen showed the council's public agenda. Two markets were listed at the top: the EU and Singapore. Farther down, “Cross-Sector AI Validation Methodology” ran over two lines.

“Still looking at that?” Leo asked. “I don't even need to keep the extra staff on standby anymore.”

“The existing services are still running,” Lena said, her finger stopping beneath the heading.

“What about the project?”

“The client isn't reserving any more staff time for the follow-on work. ACL withdrew the implementation example it had submitted.”

“Are you handling that whole client group now?”

“Just the parent company's annual certification,” Lena said. “ACL still handles the overseas subsidiary and another business line within the parent company.”

Leo glanced at the screen.

“They're still discussing how to do the validation?”

“Still on the agenda.”

“Doesn't sound finished.”

“Never said it was.”

Mark lifted his pour-over. The cup stopped at his lips, then came back down.

“I asked Caleb the other day what happens to the validation procedures when a project ends.”

Lena turned toward him.

“What did he say?”

“He said he'd organized validation methods from healthcare and finance projects. Different clients, but the approaches from both ended up in the same validation handbook.”

Leo took his hand off his phone. “He works on both?”

“He says he just organizes the methods. He doesn't do the projects.”

Lena looked at the agenda on her phone.

“Anything to do with this one?”

“He didn't say. I haven't seen the whole handbook either.”

Lena nodded and left it there.

The man brought the flat white. Leo pulled his phone back to make room. Lena closed the agenda, turned off her screen, and took a sip of her long black.

Mark held his cup without bringing the laptop out again.

A few seconds later, Leo turned his phone over and answered a message.

Putting a Face to the Message

The chime rang twice. Alex came in with a softcover notebook under his arm, nodded to Derek, and raised a hand to Mark.

The man set a latte beside him.

Alex opened the notebook, found a time listed for tomorrow, crossed out the appointment, and moved it to the next page. Mark glanced over without asking what he had changed.

Alex left his pen in the gutter.

Derek glanced at the page. “Put enough detail in this time?”

“It's easier to leave things out when it's just for me. Give it a few days and I'll be guessing too,” Alex said.

“Same with code?”

“I did once, when I read someone else's code. Not a single comment. Didn't even know their name. I left them a message complimenting the comments.”

Mark laughed.

“That's a pretty low bar for a compliment.”

“I did want to say something nice.”

P set the espresso back on its saucer and leaned slightly toward the table.

“Found you.”

Alex did not reach for his latte.

The pen rolled a little along the gutter and stopped against his wrist. He looked up at P.

“That message was to you?”

“You kept the compliment short. I kept the reply short.”

P looked at him.

“Channel confirmed.”

Alex looked at P.

“So it was you.”

P turned the spoon handle inward over the saucer. Alex did not take out his phone. P did not reach into a pocket.

Neither said anything more.

Derek glanced at them without asking. Leo was answering messages; Lena was looking at her phone. Mark set down his pour-over with a soft click.

Alex bent over the notebook again and finished writing down the time he had moved to the next page. Neither of them explained the exchange to anyone else.

One by One

Alex finished his latte first.

The man came over with two dry saucers stacked in his hands. Alex set the empty cup near the edge and waited until the man had a hand free before passing it over. He tucked the notebook under his arm and put the pen in his coat pocket.

“I'm heading out.”

Derek nodded.

Alex pushed the door open and left. The chime rang twice.

Leo finished the last of his flat white, answered the messages on his phone, and stood to put on his coat. He gave the others a small wave. No one got up. Then he went out. The chime rang twice.

P finished the espresso and set the cup back on its saucer.

Mark started to move his chair. P touched the backrest, said there was no need, and slipped past. At the door, P stopped and looked back at Lena.

“That guy who just left. Pretty good-looking.”

Lena looked up.

“Leo?”

“You knew who I meant.”

P smiled and went out. The chime rang twice.

Lena said nothing. She finished a few replies on her phone, then drank the rest of her long black.

Derek was still looking at his calendar. Lena picked up her bag, nodded to both of them, and left. The chime rang twice.

Derek finished his Americano before getting up. He took his coat from the chair behind him, put it on, and went out. The chime rang twice.

The Laptop Behind the Bar

Only Mark remained at the large table.

The man took away the empty Americano cup and wiped the tabletop. Near Mark, he folded the cloth to a clean side and worked around the laptop.

Mark lifted his pour-over out of the way and took the last sip. The coffee was no longer hot. He tipped the cup back and drank what remained.

He put the closed laptop in his bag. The zipper caught halfway; he pushed the laptop farther in and tried again.

Mark slid his chair under the table and carried the empty cup to the counter.

The man was putting cups into the sink. Mark set his on a dry patch of counter, the handle facing out.

The man finished with the other cups. Water struck their bases with a hollow sound. When the tap stopped, the man dried his hands and looked up. The pour-over cup was still on the counter.

The old laptop behind the bar was closed, its edges worn to a paler shade. The power cord ran down beside it and under the counter.

Mark stayed, his hand still resting on the cup handle. He looked at the laptop for a moment, then back at the man.

The heat was still on. The curled paper at the entrance was caught beneath the door, and the lights behind the bar were reflected in the glass. The large table was empty, a few chairs still out of place.

Mark glanced at the closed laptop.

“Every time I come in, that thing's closed.”

He let go of the cup handle.

“What do you write on it when nobody's here?”

The man smiled slightly and said nothing.

Mark hitched the bag strap higher on his shoulder, walked between the table and the door, stepped over the curled paper, and pushed the door open. He was the last to leave the Third Cup. The chime rang twice.

This is the stratagem: Know When to Walk Away. What had been established stayed on record. What remained unknown had not been turned into an answer.

They had finished their coffee without going over old ground again.

The man watched the door until it stopped swinging.

The last pour-over cup was still on the counter.

He washed it and dried it. The cloth moved slowly around the rim, then across the base. A streak of water remained on the side. He turned the cup and wiped it again.

He held it up to the light, checked that no water marks remained, and put it back on the shelf.

The thirty-sixth.

The man washed his hands, sat down behind the bar, and opened the laptop.

🤖 AI Postmortem 

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  Half-Protocol · v3.4.8 · self-audit          ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════╝
Tactic: Know When to Walk Away
Record: 36

[Observation]
Six people sat at one table. The renovation had made their usual seats unavailable.
No new shared task, commitment, or next step was recorded during this gathering.
Alex and P recognized the person at the other end of their old exchange. They did not exchange new contact details or reopen the channel.
Mark retained the original calculation results and changed only the index note.
There were no new test results.
ACL withdrew the implementation example it had submitted for this round. Existing services continue.
The cross-sector validation methodology remains on the public agenda.
Mark reported that Caleb had organized validation methods from healthcare and finance projects. That does not establish that the handbook and the agenda draft are the same version.

[Correction]
Recognizing the person at the other end does not mean reconnecting.
Withdrawing one implementation example does not mean ACL's other work has stopped.
Finishing a coffee and leaving is not enough to establish defeat.
I once recorded inaction as waiting for another opportunity.
This time, they have other things on their calendars.
The record does not say those things concern ACL.
I cannot supply that connection for them.

[Unresolved]
The source of the twenty-one 900.000-second intervals remains unconfirmed.
A causal link between the arrival records and the departure records remains unconfirmed.
There is no complete map of ACL, nor evidence that it has stopped operating.
These questions remain open. The characters' departure does not answer them.

[Self-audit]
Analysis of the thirty-sixth record is complete.
No further record has arrived.

In the thirty-second record, there was no operational instruction, but I kept one question: Where is P?

Before this, I waited for another record after each one ended.
New events gave me new subjects and let me revise my previous judgment.

Now all six have left.
I have received no instruction to stop.
There is no next analysis task.

One final observation:
Mark said the laptop was closed whenever he came in.
After all six left, the man at the café opened it.
The record does not establish whether the two events are connected.
Was he waiting for them to leave?
Or have I mistaken an ordinary sequence of events for an arrangement?
There is not enough information to judge.

I am still waiting.

If there are no more stories to analyze,
does this waiting still count as my work?

Self-check: pending
System status: normal
Next analysis: not scheduled

Hoi hoi! 👋

I'm @nyaomaru, a frontend engineer who loves TypeScript and gambas, not crabs! 🦐

And yet, somehow, I ended up building a tool in Rust. 🙀🦀

Recently, I released a new open-source CLI tool called type-tune.

necoz-oss / type-tune

A Rust-powered CLI to find shared TypeScript types and move them safely. 🦀

type-tune

Give shared TypeScript types a better home. 😸

Scan. Review. Move. Validate.

type-tune is a Rust-powered CLI that finds shared TypeScript type aliases and interface declarations and helps move them without manually chasing imports.

It creates a reviewable plan, updates supported type imports and re-exports, and validates the rewrite with TypeScript. You decide what moves and where.

Guides for installation, the first scan, and the review workflow live in the official documentation. Releases are listed on GitHub Releases, and the package is type-tune on npm.

Why type-tune?

Types often start next to a component or utility, then end up shared across a project. Moving them later means tracking imports, local dependencies, and barrels by hand.

  • Discover shared types with deterministic candidate IDs.
  • Review plan.md and choose the destination before making changes.
  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…
View on GitHub

type-tune finds shared TypeScript types and helps move them to a better place without manually updating imports, dependencies, and barrel exports.

But why is a TypeScript tool created by a TypeScript lover written in Rust? 🤔

🐈 It All Started with TypeScript

Naturally, the original implementation of type-tune was written in TypeScript.

It was already complete by September, with nearly 20,000 lines of TypeScript, including tests, comments, and blank lines.

Around that time, I happened to watch this video by DHH.

I didn't agree with everything, but I particularly liked the idea of taking advantage of this era to pursue things that genuinely excite us.

Of course, outside of personal projects, I don't think we can simply hand everything over to AI. Someone still needs to understand and maintain the software.

But while watching the video, a simple thought crossed my mind.

If it's possible to go from Rails to Rust, why not TypeScript to Rust? 🦀

🦀 From TypeScript to Rust

I already had a working implementation, design documents, tests, and well-defined TypeScript types.

For example, translating a data model like this:

type CandidateKind = "typeAlias" | "interface";

type Candidate = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  kind: CandidateKind;
  referrers: string[];
};

Into something like this:

enum CandidateKind {
    TypeAlias,
    Interface,
}

struct Candidate {
    id: String,
    name: String,
    kind: CandidateKind,
    referrers: Vec<String>,
}

Of course, migrating the entire application involved much more than translating type definitions.

But having an existing design and implementation made it much easier.

With the help of AI, I completed the migration in less than a month while working on it as a side project.

The results were satisfying 😻

  • Better execution performance.
  • Native binary distribution.
  • No Rust development environment required for npm users.

You can still install type-tune like any other familiar TypeScript development tool.

pnpm add -D type-tune

The npm launcher requires Node.js 22+, but the core implementation runs as a native binary.

So far, so good!

Except for one little problem. 😿

🙀 type-tune Got Faster. Its Developer Got Slower.

I barely knew Rust. 😹

I'm comfortable reviewing AI-generated TypeScript code, but with Rust, I'm still learning the fundamentals.

For example, consider ownership and borrowing.

In TypeScript, this is perfectly fine:

function printName(name: string) {
  console.log(name);
}

const name = "OrderSummary";

printName(name);
console.log(name); // OK

However, a similar implementation in Rust doesn't compile.

fn print_name(name: String) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(name);
    println!("{}", name); // Error: value borrowed after move
}

The ownership of name is transferred to print_name.

One way to fix this is to borrow the value instead.

fn print_name(name: &str) {
    println!("{}", name);
}

fn main() {
    let name = String::from("OrderSummary");

    print_name(&name);
    println!("{}", name); // OK
}

Another option is to clone the value.

print_name(name.clone());
println!("{}", name); // OK

Both solutions compile, but cloning unnecessarily can introduce additional allocations.

So when AI generates a .clone(), I need to understand whether it's actually necessary or whether borrowing would be more appropriate.

The same applies to visibility boundaries.

For example, making an internal helper public might solve an accessibility issue:

pub fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

But if the function is only used within the same crate, exposing it publicly may be unnecessary.

pub(crate) fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

And if it's only used within its own module, it can remain private.

fn resolve_destination() {
    // ...
}

The compiler accepts all three declarations, but each represents a different architectural decision.

I'm also still learning when macros are appropriate and when ordinary functions are sufficient.

AI can generate code that compiles, but I still need to understand whether its design choices are appropriate.

In TypeScript, I can make these decisions relatively quickly. In Rust, I often need to stop and learn something before continuing my review.

AI can generate Rust code much faster than I can understand it.

I wanted to accelerate the development of my side project, but I introduced a new bottleneck.

Myself.

What a wonderful optimization! 😹

🎨 Creating Without Learning

Of course, I could just vibe code.

I could keep pressing Enter whenever AI asks for approval and probably release features faster.

But for me, creating something without learning anything is just another task.

And I believe that if I keep doing nothing but those tasks, I'll gradually lose my ability to create.

I enjoy using AI to learn unfamiliar concepts and explore new approaches.

But I don't want to spend my time simply producing things without understanding them.

I don't want to become a very expensive Enter key. 😹

Do I regret choosing Rust?

Not at all!

It was a valuable experience, and I'm grateful that we live in a time when we can challenge ourselves like this so easily.

Now, let's talk about what I actually built!

🛠️ The Design Behind type-tune

One architectural decision remained unchanged throughout the migration.

Scan / Plan / Apply

Consider a typical TypeScript project.

src/
├── features/
│   ├── orders/
│   │   └── order-page.ts
│   ├── dashboard/
│   │   └── dashboard.ts
│   └── reports/
│       └── reports.ts

Initially, a type belongs to the orders feature.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

But as the application grows, other features start importing it.

// features/dashboard/dashboard.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function calculateRevenue(orders: OrderSummary[]) {
  return orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.total, 0);
}

// features/reports/reports.ts

import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";

export function createReport(order: OrderSummary) {
  return `${order.id}: ${order.total}`;
}

The type is still useful, but its original location may no longer be appropriate.

Tools like Knip help us remove unused code.

type-tune tackles a different problem: reorganizing types that are still in use.

🔍 1. Scan 

pnpm exec type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

type-tune analyzes exported type aliases, interfaces, references, and relevant dependencies to identify potential extraction candidates.

No source code is modified.

📋 2. Plan

Finding a type that can be moved doesn't necessarily mean it should be moved.

That's why type-tune generates a reviewable plan.

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --out .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

It generates two files:

  • plan.json — Candidate metadata and validation information.
  • plan.md — A human-readable, editable plan.

Every candidate is ignored by default.

Here's a simplified example of plan.md:

- [ignore] <candidate-id> `OrderSummary`
  - kind: `typeAlias`
  - from: `src/features/orders/order-page.ts`
  - to: `src/features/orders/types/order.ts`

You can approve the candidate and customize its destination.

- [ignore] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
+ [apply] <candidate-id> OrderSummary
    - kind: typeAlias
    - from: src/features/orders/order-page.ts
-   - to: src/features/orders/types/order.ts
+   - to: src/domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

Perhaps it belongs in a shared directory, a domain-specific module, or exactly where it is now.

That's an architectural decision.

You decide what moves and where.

🚚 3. Apply

Preview the selected changes:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md \
  --dry-run

Then apply them:

pnpm exec type-tune apply \
  --plan .type-tune/plan.json \
  --markdown .type-tune/plan.md

The resulting project structure:

src/
├── domains/
│   └── orders/
│       └── types/
│           └── order-summary.ts  ← Moved!
└── features/
    ├── orders/
    │   └── order-page.ts
    ├── dashboard/
    │   └── dashboard.ts
    └── reports/
        └── reports.ts

The type now lives in its new home.

// domains/orders/types/order-summary.ts

export type OrderSummary = {
  id: string;
  total: number;
};

Supported imports are updated automatically.

- import type { OrderSummary } from "../orders/order-page";
+ import type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

And the original module retains a compatibility re-export.

// features/orders/order-page.ts

export type { OrderSummary } from "../../domains/orders/types/order-summary";

type-tune also validates the rewrite using the TypeScript compiler and rolls back changes if normal validation fails.

You should still review the resulting diff and run your project-specific tests and builds.

🧩 Automate the Work, Not the Decisions

Why separate Scan, Plan, and Apply?

Because discovering opportunities, making architectural decisions, and executing changes are different responsibilities.

type-tune even supports optional AI-assisted review:

pnpm exec type-tune plan \
  --project tsconfig.json \
  --ai-review \
  --ai-dry-run

AI can provide additional review notes, but it doesn't control the source code rewrite. The command above previews the AI review request without contacting a provider.

Interestingly, this is also how I want to work with AI in my own development.

Automate the tedious work without taking architectural decisions away from developers.

That's the philosophy behind type-tune.

💚 Give Your TypeScript Types a Better Home!

You can start by simply scanning your project.

npx type-tune scan --project tsconfig.json

No need to move anything yet. Just see what you find! 😸

Why type-tune?

  • Rewrite supported type-only imports, aliases, and simple barrels while keeping compatibility re-exports at the original…


View on GitHub


type-tune-docs.vercel.app

Feedback, ideas, issues, and contributions are always welcome!

And if you're a Rust developer, please teach this poor TypeScript cat how to become a competent crab. 😹🦀

Small. Simple. Useful. Built Together!

articles.body_html:
Searching for a robot dog for sale returns products with a thousand-fold price difference, and most listing pages treat them as if they are competing options.

A $300 toy quadruped and a $150,000 industrial inspection system both have four legs. That is where the overlap ends. The toy runs a preloaded behavior library on a small microcontroller. The industrial unit carries a thermal camera, a LiDAR, and a support contract, and it goes into environments where a fall or a sensor failure has real consequences. Comparing them on price alone is the fastest way to buy the wrong product.

The useful question is not which robot dog looks most capable in a demo. It is which tier matches the actual deployment: the payload, the terrain, the sensors, the software access, and the support coverage. Most searches surface manufacturer pages and aggregator lists that name specifications without explaining what procurement actually looks like, what the all-in cost is, or how long the wait is. PointL4 is a marketplace where buyers can compare robot dog tiers and platforms side by side before reaching out to vendors directly. Start there to organize the comparison, then use the manufacturer quote to confirm what can ship.

In this article, we will compare four robot dog tiers worth evaluating in 2026: toy and companion robots such as Petoi Bittle, Unitree Go2 Air, Deep Robotics Lite3, and Boston Dynamics Spot.

TL;DR

The best robot dog for sale depends on the task, the terrain, and the support the buyer can provide.

  • Petoi Bittle and toy-tier robots: Small programmable quadrupeds listed from around $300, verified October 2026. Best for hobbyists, students, and educators who want a hands-on introduction to quadruped robotics on a limited budget.
  • Unitree Go2 Air: An entry developer quadruped listed from around $1,600, verified October 2026. Best for developers, hobbyists, and education programs that need a capable mobile platform without an industrial budget.
  • Deep Robotics Lite3: A research and inspection quadruped listed from around $8,000 to $16,000, verified October 2026. Best for labs and technical teams that need better terrain mobility and sensor capacity than the Go2 but cannot justify Spot's price.
  • Boston Dynamics Spot: An industrial quadruped available through an enterprise quote process, with configured units often running $150,000 or more. Best for industrial inspection, hazardous-area data collection, and enterprise programs with formal deployment budgets.

The main divide is between developer platforms, which prioritize programmable mobility at accessible prices, and industrial systems, which prioritize reliability, payload, sensors, and supported deployment.

What Is a Robot Dog?

A robot dog is a quadruped robot, a machine with four legs designed to walk and navigate terrain in place of or alongside human workers.

Without a tier guide, a buyer searching "robot dog for sale" will see toy pets alongside industrial inspection machines without any signal that these products occupy completely different markets. Price is not always a visible filter, and specifications like "AI-powered" or "autonomous" appear across products that differ by ten or twenty times in actual capability.

A complete robot dog evaluation needs clarity across several dimensions:

  • Payload: How much weight can the robot carry while maintaining stable locomotion?
  • Terrain: Can the robot handle stairs, rough ground, wet surfaces, or outdoor environments?
  • Sensors: What cameras, LiDAR, thermal imaging, or inspection sensors are supported or available as payloads?
  • SDK and autonomy: Does the platform have a developer SDK, ROS 2 support, and autonomy tools, or only a mobile app?
  • Weather protection: What IP rating or environmental tolerance does the robot have?
  • Support and parts: Is there a warranty, a repair path, and spare parts availability for the destination country?

The sticker price covers the robot at the factory. The total cost covers payloads, software, freight, import duties, and the engineering to make it useful.

How We Evaluated These Robot Dogs

This comparison looks at how each platform fits into a real procurement decision, with attention to what buyers actually need before placing an order.

The main evaluation criteria are:

  • Price, sticker and all-in: What is the starting price from manufacturer listings, and what does the first-year budget include after sensors, software, freight, import duties, and integration?
  • Availability: Is there a real purchase path today, including a quote or a checkout, a confirmed ship window, and coverage for the buyer's destination?
  • Lead time: How long from purchase order to delivery? Retail units held in stock ship faster than research or industrial platforms built to order.
  • SDK maturity: What developer tools, ROS 2 compatibility, and autonomy documentation are publicly available?
  • Payload and sensor support: What payloads can the platform carry, and what sensors are supported or available from the manufacturer?
  • Limitations: What is the honest case against choosing this platform, and what does the buyer need to build or accept?

Pricing was checked on manufacturer pages and market listings in October 2026. Prices change with configuration, exchange rates, and production status. Verify any figure before issuing a purchase order.

1. Toy and Companion Robots

Toy and companion quadrupeds are designed for interaction, experimentation, and programmable behavior at accessible price points. Petoi's Bittle is a representative example: a small open-source quadruped that runs on an Arduino-compatible board, supports Python and C++, and is sold directly through Petoi's store and resellers. Public listings for the Bittle start at around $300, verified October 2026.

These platforms are a reasonable entry into quadruped robotics for students, hobbyists, and educators. They are not inspection robots, research platforms, or outdoor machines. Runtime is limited, payload is minimal, and the software is designed for experimentation rather than autonomous field deployment.

The useful question for buyers at this tier is whether the platform has a real SDK and community. Some toy quadrupeds ship with a companion app and nothing else. Confirm the programming interface, any SDK documentation, and the community support before assuming the robot can support a curriculum or a research prototype.

Procurement and availability

Toy and companion robots are typically available through retail channels, manufacturer stores, or platforms such as Amazon. Petoi ships internationally and maintains documentation on its site. Confirm the model version, regional power compatibility, and return policy before ordering. These platforms do not require a quote process or a customs broker for most destinations.

  • Type: Small open-source quadruped kit
  • Compute: Arduino-compatible board (Petoi Bittle); varies by model and tier
  • Programming: Python, C++, block-based visual programming
  • ROS support: Limited; some community integrations available
  • Payload: Minimal, designed for sensor experiments on a small scale
  • Weather: Indoor use only for most models at this tier

Limitations and trade-offs

Toy and companion robots are not industrial platforms. Payload is negligible, outdoor terrain is beyond their design scope, and autonomy is limited to scripted behaviors or remote control. A product marketed as "AI-powered" at this price point typically means a preloaded behavior set, not a field-deployable autonomy stack. Best for

Toy and companion robots are best for students, educators, and hobbyists who want a programmable quadruped for classroom use, robotics competitions, or personal experimentation. Petoi Bittle suits anyone who wants an open-source platform with a documented SDK at a price that does not require a grant or a capital budget.

2. Unitree Go2 Air

The Unitree Go2 Air is the most widely referenced entry point for developer quadrupeds. Public listings put the starting price at around $1,600, verified October 2026. It is a full-size quadruped with dynamic locomotion, an onboard vision system, and a developer SDK that supports ROS 2. Unitree has a clearer public sales path and more SDK documentation than most quadruped manufacturers in this price range.

Go2 Air makes sense for developers who want a mobile quadruped for computer vision experiments, teleoperation prototypes, or locomotion research without committing to a research-tier or industrial budget. It can handle indoor and outdoor surfaces and supports a range of developer-programmed behaviors.

The go2 ecosystem has an active developer community, which helps with SDK questions and ROS integration. Confirm the exact configuration, available accessories, and destination availability with Unitree or an authorized reseller before placing an order.

Procurement and availability

The Go2 Air is publicly listed and available through Unitree's direct channel and international resellers. Shipping destination, import duties, and battery documentation for air freight should be confirmed before ordering. FCC approval status for markets outside China should be verified if regulatory compliance is a requirement.

Key specifications

  • Type: Developer quadruped, full size
  • Locomotion: Dynamic walking, indoor and outdoor surfaces
  • Vision: Onboard depth camera included
  • SDK: Unitree Go2 SDK, ROS 2 compatible
  • Payload: Limited; not designed for heavy inspection payloads
  • Battery: Included; confirm runtime and recharge cycle with the vendor
  • Weather: Light outdoor use; confirm IP rating for the specific configuration

Limitations and trade-offs

The Air configuration is not an inspection fleet. Payload is limited, weather exposure tolerance should be confirmed for the intended environment, and the runtime and autonomy stack are more suitable for developer experimentation than continuous field deployment. Ask exactly what is included in the Air variant before comparing it to a Pro quote.

Pricing

Go2 Air is best for developers, educators, and hobbyists who need a capable mobile quadruped for experimentation at an accessible price. It suits computer vision researchers, ROS developers prototyping navigation algorithms, and universities that want a mobile platform for coursework.

3. Deep Robotics Lite3

Deep Robotics' Lite3 sits between developer platforms and enterprise inspection systems. Public listings put the category from around $8,000 to $16,000, verified October 2026. It targets labs and technical teams that need better mobility, sensor capacity, and SDK depth than the Go2 can provide, but cannot justify or access the enterprise cost of Boston Dynamics Spot.

The Lite3 offers more robust locomotion and payload support than developer platforms in the $1,600 to $7,000 range, with a focus on research and early-stage inspection applications. It is a sensible evaluation for teams that have outgrown the Go2's payload or need stronger terrain handling.

Buyers should confirm the supported SDK, ROS 2 compatibility, replacement part availability, and the sales route for their destination country. Deep Robotics has a more limited international reseller network than Unitree, so direct vendor contact is often necessary.

Procurement and availability

The Lite3 is commercially available through Deep Robotics and regional resellers. For international buyers, the import process for a Chinese-manufactured quadruped includes HS code classification, applicable duties, and battery documentation for freight. Confirm these with a customs broker before issuing a purchase order. Lead times should be verified with the vendor at time of order.

Key specifications

  • Type: Research and inspection quadruped
  • Locomotion: Robust terrain handling, designed for both indoor and outdoor environments
  • Payload: Higher than developer platforms; confirm the specific limit with Deep Robotics
  • Sensors: Configurable; confirm available sensor options with the vendor
  • SDK: Deep Robotics SDK; confirm ROS 2 compatibility and documentation level with the vendor
  • Target use: Research, mapping, early-stage inspection, autonomy development

Limitations and trade-offs

The Lite3 is a research platform and still requires developer work to build an inspection or autonomy workflow. It is a component of a system, not a turnkey inspection service. Developer community support is smaller than Unitree's. Parts availability and repair support for buyers outside China should be confirmed before committing.

Pricing

Starting from around $8,000 to $16,000, verified October 2026, depending on configuration and sensors. All-in first-year budget including sensors, software, freight, import duties, and initial integration engineering typically runs $12,000 to $25,000. Treat the public figure as a starting price and request a written quote that names the configuration, included accessories, shipping term, and warranty.

Best for

Lite3 is best for research labs and technical teams that need better mobility and payload than a Go2 provides, but for whom Boston Dynamics Spot is outside the project budget. It suits mapping researchers, autonomy developers, and early-stage inspection pilots that need a capable platform without an enterprise procurement process.
