4. Boston Dynamics Spot

Boston Dynamics Spot is the benchmark for industrial quadruped deployment. The often-repeated $74,500 figure is a stale starting price from 2020 and should not be used for any current budget planning. Boston Dynamics now quotes Spot as a configured system through its enterprise sales process. Configured units with payloads, software, training, and support frequently reach $150,000 or more, and full enterprise deployments can go well beyond that. Verify the current configuration and pricing directly with Boston Dynamics.

Spot is relevant to industrial inspection, hazardous-area data collection, and structured enterprise programs that can support a formal deployment. Its value is in the combination of robust locomotion, a wide payload ecosystem, enterprise-grade software, and a support model designed for organizations that need the robot to be available continuously rather than only for experiments.

The buyer at this tier is not looking for a developer platform. They are starting a deployment project with a defined use case, an integration budget, and an engineering team or a system integrator.

Procurement and availability

Spot is available through an enterprise sales process, with a quote required. Boston Dynamics works with buyers and system integrators to scope configured systems, payloads, software, training, and support. Production and delivery timelines depend on the configuration and the program scope. Do not use the 2020 sticker price as a planning figure. Request a detailed proposal that names the configuration, payloads, software, Incoterm, and support contract.

Key specifications

  • Type: Industrial quadruped for enterprise deployment
  • Payload: Up to 14 kg; supports thermal cameras, LiDAR, inspection cameras, and manipulator arm
  • SDK: Spot SDK with Python and C++ bindings, REST API, ROS 2 compatible
  • Autonomy: Supports autonomous inspection routes, data collection, and fleet management
  • Weather: IP54 rated, designed for outdoor and industrial environments
  • Software: Spot Enterprise with fleet management, mission planning, and remote operations
  • Support: Formal service contract; warranty and repair managed through Boston Dynamics

Limitations and trade-offs

Total cost is the primary limitation. A configured unit, payloads, software, training, support, and integration engineering can push the project well beyond the hardware line. A formal deployment also requires operator training, a safe operating environment, a data handling plan, and a defined process for maintenance and recovery. Buyers who need a research platform or want to experiment with quadruped autonomy should start with a Go2 or Lite3 and graduate to Spot when the use case justifies the investment.

Pricing

Starting from around $150,000 or more for a configured deployment, verified October 2026 based on enterprise deployment references and market reporting. The often-cited $74,500 price is a 2020 sticker for a base unit and does not reflect current configured pricing. Do not include the old sticker figure in any budget document. Request an itemized proposal from Boston Dynamics that includes all payloads, software licenses, training, and support contract terms.

Best for

Spot is best for industrial operators, energy companies, manufacturing facilities, and enterprise buyers who have a defined inspection, data collection, or hazardous-area task, an engineering team or system integrator for deployment, and a formal procurement process with acceptance criteria.

Explore Boston Dynamics Spot

How to Choose the Right Robot Dog

Choosing a robot dog starts with the task and the environment, not the price or the brand recognition.

  • What is the environment?

Indoor floors, construction sites, plant rooms, outdoor rough terrain, stairs, rain, dust, and radio restrictions all affect the right choice. A Go2 Air handles indoor and light outdoor use. Spot is rated for industrial environments. Confirm the IP rating and terrain capability before shortlisting any platform.

  • What payload and runtime does the task require?

Write down the sensor or arm, target carry weight, required walking duration, and whether the robot needs to operate continuously under load. A developer quadruped at $1,600 carries little payload and has limited runtime. An industrial system at $150,000 carries up to 14 kg with sensor fusion for continuous inspection.

  • Does the SDK match the team's workflow?

Ask whether ROS 2 is supported, whether simulation tools are available, and whether autonomous behaviors require a separate license or vendor service. A platform with poor SDK documentation adds significant engineering time.

  • What does the total first-year cost look like, not just the sticker price?

Add the base platform, sensors, compute, software, freight, import duties if applicable, and integration engineering. A $3,000 research quadruped can require a laptop, spare batteries, a charger, and software work. An industrial system adds payloads, fleet software, training, and support.

  • Is there a real purchase path today?

Verify that there is a seller, a written quote, and a delivery schedule before treating any platform as available. "Available" on a product page can mean available to order, not physically ready to ship to your address. Get a ship window in writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does a robot dog for sale cost?
Toy and companion robots start from around $100 to $800. Developer platforms such as the Unitree Go2 Air are listed from around $1,600. Research quadrupeds like the Deep Robotics Lite3 run $8,000 to $16,000. Industrial systems such as Boston Dynamics Spot require a quote and commonly cost $150,000 or more for a configured deployment. Prices were verified October 2026 and should be confirmed directly before ordering.

Can I buy a robot dog for industrial inspection?
Yes, but an industrial purchase is an enterprise quote rather than a retail checkout. Confirm payloads, thermal or LiDAR options, weather limits, autonomy capabilities, fleet software, training, repair support, and acceptance testing. A research quadruped may be cheaper to start with, but you will need to build the inspection workflow and support process yourself.

How long does a robot dog take to arrive?
Retail-tier units can ship within days when a local reseller has inventory. Research and industrial platforms often take weeks or months, especially with custom payloads. Ask for a written ship window tied to the exact configuration. "Available" can mean available to order, not physically ready for your address.

Is the Boston Dynamics Spot price really $74,500?
No. That price is from 2020 and should not be used for any current budget. Configured Spot deployments with payloads, software, training, and support commonly reach $150,000 or more as of October 2026. Request a current quote directly from Boston Dynamics that itemizes the configuration, payloads, software licenses, training, and support contract.

Is PointL4 selling these robot dogs directly?
PointL4 is a marketplace for comparing humanoid robots and advanced physical AI hardware including robot dogs. Use it to compare platforms by tier, use case, and price before reaching out to vendors. Then verify the seller, configuration, availability, lead time, and purchase terms before ordering.

Final Thoughts

The right robot dog is the one whose payload, sensors, software, and support coverage match the job. A toy quadruped and an industrial inspection machine are not competing products. Choosing the right tier before evaluating specific models saves time and prevents a costly mismatch between what the demo shows and what the deployment requires.

For hobbyists and educators, Petoi Bittle and toy-tier platforms are the realistic starting point. For developers who need a capable mobile quadruped without industrial pricing, the Unitree Go2 Air delivers. For research teams that need more sensors and compute, the Go2 Pro or the Deep Robotics Lite3 are the serious options to compare. For enterprise inspection and hazardous-area programs, Boston Dynamics Spot is the benchmark, with a current configured price that reflects the full deployment scope rather than a 2020 sticker.

Before making a decision, verify the current price, availability, and lead time at the manufacturer's site. articles.title: Here Lie My Side Projects.
articles.description: I did not plan a funeral. I opened a folder.  It was a Sunday, the kind where the light comes in...
articles.body_html:
I did not plan a funeral. I opened a folder.

It was a Sunday, the kind where the light comes in sideways and you can hear the neighbours' television through the wall, and I was looking for a file I had lost. A photo, actually. A screenshot of a receipt I needed. I never found it. I found the graveyard instead. That is how it goes with folders. You go in looking for one thing and come out carrying something else. Inside the folder called "projects" were four folders I had not opened in months, and one I had never opened at all. I sat there for a minute, looking at them, and then I counted. Four projects. Four starts. Four endings I never noticed happening.

So I walked through them, one by one, the way you walk through a graveyard when you have nowhere else to be. Each one has a stone. Here they are.

HABITRACK — March to March.
Cause of death: the settings page.
Last words: "fix streak counter (again)"

This was the first one, and the one I loved most. The idea was simple: a page where you tick off your habits and watch a little flame grow. I built the flame first. Of course I built the flame first. The flame was orange and it flickered when you ticked a box, and for three days I was the kind of person who ticks boxes. The flame had three sizes. Small for three days, medium for seven, big for thirty. I never saw big. Nobody saw big. Big is still in the code, waiting, like a room nobody has ever slept in. I used it myself for nine days. Nine days of morning walks and water and reading before bed, and then I missed a day. One day, a Tuesday, nothing dramatic, I just forgot. And the flame went out, and I could not face lighting it again. The flame was supposed to keep me going. Instead it kept score. I opened the settings page to add a "forgive one missed day" button, saw what the settings page needed, toggles, defaults, a whole second app hiding inside the first one, and closed the laptop. That was March. The streak counter is still broken. The commit message says "(again)" because I had fixed it twice before, and both times it broke in a new way, and the third time I wrote "(again)" the way you sigh in text form.

THE RECIPE BOX — June to July.
Cause of death: the login form.
Last words: "add search (basic)"

Twelve recipes. All mine. The lentil soup, the fried rice, the chicken curry I make when people come over and I want them to think I have my life together. I photographed every dish, in my own kitchen, on my own chipped plate. The photos were the fun part. The search box was the fun part too. Type "lentil" and the soup appears, like a trick. Then I realised that if anyone else was ever going to use it, they would need an account, and accounts need passwords, and passwords need reset emails, and reset emails need a whole machine I did not want to build. I sat there one evening, looking at the login form I had started — two empty boxes and a button that did nothing — and I understood something I did not want to understand: I did not want to build the login form. I wanted to cook the soup. I closed the laptop and cooked the soup. The search still says "(basic)" in the commit message. The search was fine. The search was never the problem.

BUDGET BUDDY — September to September.
Cause of death: the bank statement.
Last words: "wip: csv import"

This one died the fastest, and I respect it for that. The idea: upload your bank statement, see where your money goes, feel like an adult. The fun part was the pie chart. I made a pie chart with seven colours and I stared at it for a long time, the way you stare at a cake you baked yourself. Then I tried to import a real statement, and the bank's file had columns in an order I had never seen, and dates in a format from another century, and one row that just said "MISC" with no amount at all. I spent a Saturday afternoon writing code to understand one bank's idea of a spreadsheet, and by the evening I had a headache and a new respect for accountants. The next morning I opened a plain spreadsheet, typed my spending into it by hand, and it took fourteen minutes. Fourteen minutes, and it worked. Budget Buddy is still in the folder, with its beautiful pie chart and its one broken import. The spreadsheet has no pie chart. The spreadsheet works.

FLASHCARDS — October to November.
Cause of death: card number thirteen.
Last words: "add deck: spanish basics (12 cards)"

The flip animation was the whole project, if I am honest. A card that turns over when you tap it, smooth as a coin trick. I built the flip in an evening and showed it to everyone I knew. Then I had to fill it with cards, and filling it meant typing, and typing meant sitting down and typing two hundred words I did not know into little boxes. I got to twelve. Twelve cards of Spanish basics: hola, gracias, buenos días, and nine more I have mostly forgotten. I remember three now. Hola, gracias, and buenos días. The card that killed it was number thirteen. I sat there, looking at the empty box, and I could not think of a thirteenth word. Not because I did not know one. Because I knew that after thirteen would come fourteen, and after fourteen, a hundred and eighty-six more. I closed the laptop. The flip animation still works. It is beautiful. It flips twelve cards.

There was a fifth. It has one commit, called "initial commit," and no stone. Some projects do not even get a funeral. I do not remember what it was supposed to be. The folder is called "notes-app-final-v2." The name is the whole story. Final. Version two. There was a version one, and it is not in the folder, and I do not remember deleting it.

I sat with the graveyard for a while. Four stones, one unmarked, and a folder full of almosts. Then I did something I had not planned. I opened the oldest one, Habitrack, March, the flame, and I fixed the streak counter. Really fixed it, not the "(again)" kind. It took twenty minutes. Twenty minutes, for a bug I had carried around for eight months. Then I added the button I had never built: "forgive one missed day." One button. No settings page. No toggles. Just a button that says: it is fine. You missed a day. The flame stays lit.

I sat with the link for a while before I sent it. Sending it felt bigger than building it had, which is a strange thing to feel about a page with one button and a flame. But I sent it anyway. Three friends. No announcement, no launch, no post about it. Just a message: "I made this ages ago. It's ugly. It works. Don't judge the flame."

That evening, Rafi sent me a screenshot. Seven days. A little flame, lit, on his phone. "Day 7," he wrote. "Still going."

I looked at the screenshot for a long time. The flame was lit. Just not on my phone.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam
