articles.body_html:
If you run Docker on more than one machine, you probably know the routine: SSH into a box, cd into a folder, docker compose ps, tail some logs, repeat on the next server. It works, but it does not scale well once you have a handful of hosts and a few dozen stacks.

Arcane is an open-source, self-hosted web UI for Docker and Docker Compose that tries to fix that without making you learn a new orchestration model. It sits on top of the Docker you already have and gives you a dashboard, a Compose editor, logs, a terminal, and multi-host management from one place.

This article covers what Arcane is, how to get it running, and the details that matter when you move past "it works on my laptop."

What Arcane is (and is not)

Arcane is:

  • A web UI for Docker and Compose. Containers, images, volumes, networks, and Compose "projects" (stacks) are all first-class.
  • Self-hosted, single container. You run it next to your workloads and talk to Docker through the socket (or a socket proxy).
  • Open source under BSD-3-Clause. No paid tiers, no feature gating.
  • Built with Go and SvelteKit. The backend is Go, the frontend is SvelteKit with TypeScript.

Arcane is not:

  • An orchestrator. It does not replace Kubernetes or Swarm scheduling. It manages Docker and Compose the way you already use them.
  • A new config format. Your stacks stay as normal compose.yaml files on disk. If you stop using Arcane tomorrow, docker compose up -d still works.

That last point is the main reason a lot of developers are trying it. There is no lock-in. Arcane reads and writes standard Compose files.

Feature overview

Here is what you get out of the box:

Area What you get
Containers Start, stop, restart, inspect, real-time logs, web terminal, process list
Compose projects Create and edit stacks in the browser, deploy, pull, redeploy
Images Browse, pull, prune, browse registry repos and tags, build workspace
Networks Management plus an interactive network topology view
Multi-host Manage remote Docker hosts through agents (direct or edge mode)
GitOps Point Arcane at a Git repo and sync stacks from it
Updates Tag-based auto-updates with an optional cool-down delay
Security Trivy vulnerability scanning, image patching with Copacetic
Auth Local users, OIDC/SSO, passkeys, MFA, role mappings
Ops Scheduled volume and S3 backups, OpenTelemetry export
Automation REST API and a Go-based CLI (arcane-cli)
Runtimes Docker, plus Podman (rootful, rootless, and quadlets)

Quick start

You need Docker and Docker Compose on the host.

1. Generate an encryption key

Arcane requires a 32-byte ENCRYPTION_KEY. Either of these works:

openssl rand -hex 32

docker run --rm ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/manager:v2 /app/arcane generate secret

2. Create compose.yaml 

services:
  arcane:
    image: ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/manager:v2
    container_name: arcane
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "3552:3552"
    environment:
      - APP_URL=http://localhost:3552
      - ENCRYPTION_KEY=replace-with-your-generated-key
      - PROJECTS_DIRECTORY=/opt/stacks
      - TZ=UTC
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - arcane-data:/app/data
      - /opt/stacks:/opt/stacks

volumes:
  arcane-data:

3. Start it 

docker compose up -d

Open http://<your-host>:3552 and log in with the default credentials:

  • Username: arcane
  • Password: arcane-admin

You will be forced to change the password on first login.

Things developers should know

The quick start gets you running. These are the details that save you time later.

1. Use the current image name and pin v2

The image moved from ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/arcane to ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/manager. Many older blog posts and templates still use the old name. Official mirrors also exist on Docker Hub (getarcaneapp/manager) and Quay (quay.io/getarcaneapp/manager).

Pin the v2 tag for anything you care about. Avoid latest and any beta tags in production.

2. Keep host and container paths identical for stacks

Notice the stacks volume above: /opt/stacks:/opt/stacks. Compose files often use relative paths for bind mounts (./data:/data). When Arcane runs docker compose from inside its container, those paths are resolved against the Docker host, not the Arcane container.

Arcane can translate mismatched paths now, but mounting the same path on both sides is still the recommended setup and avoids surprises. PROJECTS_DIRECTORY also accepts a <containerPath>:<hostPath> form if you need them to differ.

3. Mounting the Docker socket is root-equivalent

Anything with access to /var/run/docker.sock can effectively control the host. That is true for Arcane and for every other Docker UI.

For hardened setups, put a socket proxy in front of Docker and point Arcane at it:

environment:
  - DOCKER_HOST=tcp://docker-socket-proxy:2375

Then remove the socket mount from the Arcane service. Two common proxies are wollomatic/socket-proxy (deny-by-default) and Tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy. Take the exact allow-list from Arcane's socket proxy docs rather than guessing.

One gotcha: if you use wollomatic/socket-proxy with -allowfrom, include arcane-upgrader as well as arcane. Self-upgrades run through a helper with that alias and will fail without it.

4. Every secret supports _FILE

Any sensitive variable can be read from a file by adding _FILE. This plays well with Docker secrets:

environment:
  - ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/arcane_encryption_key
secrets:
  - arcane_encryption_key

Also note that JWT_SECRET from older guides is no longer used in 2.x. Arcane generates and stores its own session signing key. If you still set JWT_SECRET, you just get a warning at startup, so remove it.

5. Behind a reverse proxy, set TRUSTED_PROXIES and APP_URL

If Arcane sits behind Nginx, Traefik, Caddy, or a Cloudflare Tunnel:

  • Set APP_URL to the public URL (for example https://arcane.example.com, no port).
  • Set TRUSTED_PROXIES to the CIDR of your proxy. Without it, client IPs in logs and rate limiting will be wrong.
  • Make sure WebSockets are passed through. Logs and the terminal depend on them. In Nginx that means proxy_http_version 1.1 plus the Upgrade and Connection "upgrade" headers.

Minimal Nginx location block:

location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3552;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
}

Arcane can also serve HTTPS itself with TLS_ENABLED, TLS_CERT_FILE, and TLS_KEY_FILE if you prefer not to run a proxy.

6. Managing multiple hosts: direct vs edge agents

To manage other servers, run the Arcane agent (ghcr.io/getarcaneapp/agent) on each one. There are two modes:

  • Direct mode. The manager connects to the agent on TCP port 3553. Simple, but the agent must be reachable from the manager.
  • Edge mode. The agent dials out to the manager over mTLS. No inbound port is needed on the remote host, which makes it a good fit for machines behind NAT or a home router.

You do not need to write the agent config by hand. In the UI, go to Environments > Add Environment and Arcane generates a token and a ready-to-paste Compose snippet.

Edge agents support several transports through EDGE_TRANSPORT:

  • auto (default): gRPC tunnel with WebSocket fallback
  • grpc or websocket: force one tunnel type
  • poll: periodic check-in with no persistent tunnel, useful behind Cloudflare Tunnel or strict proxies

An agent in poll mode shows as Standby when idle. That is normal and means it is healthy.

If you run Traefik in front of the manager with edge agents on auto or grpc, disable the entrypoint read timeout, otherwise tunnels drop after about 60 seconds.

7. GitOps without a CI pipeline

You can point Arcane at a Git repository that contains your Compose files and it will keep the stacks in sync. For small teams and home labs this is often enough to get a "push to deploy" flow without setting up webhooks or a CI runner. Use SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS to pin host keys when cloning over SSH.

8. Auto-updates with a safety delay

Arcane can update containers when a new image is published for the tag you track. To reduce the risk of pulling a compromised or broken image the minute it lands, you can set an update delay in hours.

Per project, in your Compose file:

x-arcane:
  updater:
    delay: 72

Or per container, with a label:

labels:
  - com.getarcaneapp.arcane.updater.delay=72

A value of 0 on a service opts it out of the delay.

9. Automate it: API and CLI

Arcane exposes a REST API, and there is a Go CLI for scripting:

go install github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane/cli/v2@latest

For automation, ADMIN_STATIC_API_KEY lets you provision a fixed API key through the environment instead of creating one in the UI.

10. Use SSO if you share it with a team

OIDC is configured under Settings > Authentication or through environment variables (OIDC_ENABLED, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, OIDC_ISSUER_URL, OIDC_SCOPES). The redirect URI is:

https://<your-arcane-url>/auth/oidc/callback

You can map IdP group claims to Arcane roles with OIDC_ROLE_MAPPINGS, including per-environment roles. If you ever lock yourself out, a local backup login is available at /login/backup.

A small but common mistake: when you use the list form of environment: in Compose, do not wrap OIDC values in quotes. The quotes become part of the value and discovery fails.

Useful environment variables

Variable Purpose Default
ENCRYPTION_KEY Required 32-byte key for encrypting stored secrets none
APP_URL Public URL of the UI http://localhost:3552
PROJECTS_DIRECTORY Where Compose projects live /app/data/projects
DOCKER_HOST Docker endpoint, use tcp:// for a socket proxy unix:///var/run/docker.sock
PUID / PGID User and group the app runs as 65532
TRUSTED_PROXIES CIDR of reverse proxies unset
DATABASE_URL Database connection SQLite
TLS_ENABLED Serve HTTPS directly false
LOG_LEVEL Log verbosity info
TZ Time zone system

If the container cannot talk to the Docker socket because of permissions, either run it as root or add the host's docker group ID with group_add.

How it compares

Arcane overlaps with tools like Portainer, Dockge, and Komodo. A rough way to think about it:

  • Portainer is the long-standing, broad option, with some features in paid editions.
  • Dockge focuses narrowly on Compose stack editing on a single host.
  • Arcane aims for a modern UI with Compose at the center, built-in multi-host agents, GitOps, security scanning, and SSO, all under a permissive open-source license with no paid tier.

The best choice depends on how many hosts you run and how much you want built in. Arcane is easy to try side by side with whatever you use now, since it works on plain Compose files.

Links:

  • Repository: https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane

If you try it, share your setup in the comments. I am curious how people are running it across multiple hosts.

articles.title: Stop Counting Tools. Start Counting Turns.
articles.description: Two days ago I measured what 200 tools cost an agent before it does any work: 24,522 tokens per...
articles.body_html:
Two days ago I measured what 200 tools cost an agent before it does any work: 24,522 tokens per message, 122.6 per tool, a straight line with no bulk discount. The comments on that piece kept asking the same follow-up, and paul_irolla asked it sharpest: per-message tokens are the menu, not the bill. The bill is per solved task, and the schema goes back over the wire on every turn, so its cost is size times turns. He measures that on THOL, the leaderboard he maintains, and he pointed me at its published per-run data. So I took his data, all 4,310 runs of it, and sliced it myself by tool-list size instead of trusting the board's grouping.

The first thing I found undoes half the question. There is no 200-tool entry in THOL. The biggest real tool list anyone measured there is 30 tools. My 200-tool number was a synthetic server I built in the morning; nobody in this data runs anything like it. So this piece answers the question the data can actually answer: what does a list of 0, 8, 13 and 30 tools cost per solved task, on the same tasks, same model, same board? And the answer argues with the piece I wrote two days ago.

My claim is this: the size of the list does not decide the bill. What the tools do does. A 30-tool list costs about the same per solved task as no list at all. A 13-tool list costs 41% more. If you are counting tools to predict your bill, you are counting the wrong thing.

The numbers

THOL publishes every run: the task, the tool, whether it solved it, the tokens, the turns, the cost. The board groups rows by how big the run was, not by how many tools the list held, which is why paul_irolla said to slice it ourselves. The only list-size field in the data is the count of tools each tool's own server exposes, and only three of the thirteen entries expose a server at all: codegraph with 8 tools, lean-ctx with 13, code-review-graph with 30. Everything else works through a hook, a proxy, a prompt or a command line, and vanilla Claude Code, the control, runs with none. I sliced the board's own headline set, the 17 long tasks where a run burns more than 200,000 tokens, on the campaign the board's own table uses, 170 runs per entry, the same 17 tasks for all four. Then I ran the same slice over both campaigns in the file as a check, and the shape held.

List Tools Tokens per solved task Turns per solved task Cost per solved task
Vanilla Claude Code 0 301,467 16.95 $0.5426
codegraph 8 294,318 17.60 $0.5367
code-review-graph 30 304,341 17.80 $0.5221
lean-ctx 13 425,411 22.43 $0.5614

Read the first three rows twice. Zero tools, 301,467 tokens per solved task. Eight tools, 294,318, down 2.4%. Thirty tools, 304,341, up 1.0%. The list nearly quadruples and the bill does not move. Then the 13-tool list arrives at 425,411, up 41%, with five and a half extra turns per solved task. The expensive list is not the big one. It is the middle one, and the reason is not its size.

One more check before the argument, because means lie. The median run tells a slightly different story: vanilla 167,766 tokens, codegraph 191,700, code-review-graph 198,273, lean-ctx 310,098. On medians the two lists cost 14% and 18% more than vanilla, not nothing, and lean-ctx is 85% more. But the board's own noise floor says a run varies by about 17% from one attempt to the next, so a gap of a few percent between rows is not a ranking, it is weather. The lean-ctx gap is far outside that weather. The other two are inside it.

Problem 1: the rent is real, and it is small next to the run

Two days ago I showed the rent: 122.6 tokens per tool, per message. At 30 tools that is about 3,700 tokens a message. Over 17 turns that is roughly 60,000 tokens of rent inside a 304,000-token run, and most of it arrives as cached re-reads, billed cheap. At 8 tools it is about 1,000 a message, 17,000 over the run. The difference between the two lists is real money, a few cents a task, and it vanishes inside the noise of a run that burns 300,000 tokens. The rent matters, but only when the list gets big enough to matter, and nobody in this data runs a list big enough. That is the honest reconciliation with my own earlier piece: the per-message line is straight and true, and at the sizes anyone actually runs, the run itself is the bill.

Where do those 300,000 tokens actually go? Barely any of it is fresh input, about 0%, and barely any of it is output, about 2%. Between 90% and 92% of it is cache re-reads: the model reading the same growing context back on every turn. Every extra turn re-reads everything that came before it. That is why the turn count, not the list size, is the number to watch.

Problem 2: the most-used tool is the most expensive one

Lean-ctx is the one tool in the whole board the agent actually calls. In 154 of its 170 runs, about 11 calls a run. Every other entry sits near zero: codegraph's tools were called in 4 of 170 runs, code-review-graph's in none at all. And lean-ctx still came out the most expensive, by a distance. Being used is necessary, the board's own write-up says so, but it is not sufficient. What the tool returns has to be worth more than the tokens it costs to offer it and to read it, and when the returns are poor the agent falls back to its normal way of working, re-reading and re-searching, which costs turns. Lean-ctx paid the adoption price and then paid the fallback price on top. Eleven calls a run, five and a half extra turns, 41% more tokens. Use is not a win. Use that works is a win.

Problem 3: the list nobody calls costs nothing

Code-review-graph is my favourite row in the whole file, because it is the cleanest test in it. Thirty tools offered, never called once, in 170 runs. Its bill on the mean is 1% above vanilla, inside the noise. That is the pure standing cost of a 30-tool list: about nothing. So the fear that kept me counting tools, that merely offering a long list would quietly tax every turn, does not survive contact with this data, at 30 tools at least. The list you never use costs nothing. The list you use badly costs everything. The difference is not the count. It is the call.

Problem 4: per solved task is nearly per run here, and that is a caveat, not a trick

One more honest note, because the denominator matters. Of the 4,310 runs in the file, 4,309 solved their task. One failed. So "per solved task" is effectively "per run" in this data, and the solved-task framing barely moves any number. That is not a flaw in the slice, but it is a limit on what it proves: these tasks are near-always solved by this model, so the data cannot tell you what a hard task costs when the agent fails twice before succeeding. The per-solved-task bill on genuinely hard work is still an open question, and it is a better one than the one I answered.

What would change my mind: a real 200-tool entry in this data, or any data. At 200 tools the rent stops being a rounding error, about 24,500 tokens a message, 17 turns, and the standing cost alone would be a six-figure token pile before the agent does anything. My earlier piece measured that rent on a synthetic server. This piece shows that nobody has published a real run at that size. Until someone does, "big lists are expensive" is a true statement about a menu nobody has ordered from.

If you run agents with a long tool list, what does your bill actually track, the list size, the turns, or something else entirely? And what is the biggest list you have run in real work, not in a test?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Dialogs don't need JavaScript anymore. Tabs still do.
articles.description: I turned JavaScript off, opened a demo built to work without it, and went looking for the one thing...
articles.body_html:
I turned JavaScript off, opened a demo built to work without it, and went looking for the one thing that broke.

I found it in the sidebar. The user's email address reads "[email protected]". The copy of the same page in its GitHub repo says alex@example.com. Cloudflare rewrote the address on its way out and added the page's only <script> tag to decode it again.

Everything else on the page worked. The demo is the example page for Alloy CSS, a stylesheet that hit 181 points on Show HN yesterday with a simple pitch: dialogs, menus and tabs that keep working with scripts off. The author, Fandy Pradana, ended his post with "Tell me where it breaks." So I did what he asked, and I think the answer draws a line every server-rendered app can use.

What I clicked, with scripts off

The example is one screen of a made-up invoicing app: a sidebar, a table of invoices, a "New invoice" modal, five popover menus and drawers, tabs over four lists, a bulk action bar and a toast. I drove it with headless Chromium 151 through Playwright, JavaScript disabled for the whole session, and logged what each click did:

script requests with JS off: 0
dialog open after click: true
page scroll locked: hidden
dialog open after Esc: false
range menu open: true
row ticked: true
bulk bar visible after tick: true
toast open: true
toast open after its close button: false
panels visible after Overdue: [false,true,false,false]

Zero script requests, so Cloudflare's decoder never loaded either. That's why the email stayed scrambled.

None of this is a trick. The browser does the work, and the stylesheet styles it. A button opens a real <dialog> with two attributes:

<button type="button" commandfor="confirm" command="show-modal">Delete</button>
<dialog id="confirm" closedby="any" class="dialog">...</dialog>

The menus are popover elements placed under their button with CSS anchor positioning (position-area). The page stops scrolling behind the modal because of one rule, html:has(dialog:modal). The bulk bar appears because its wrapper matches :has(input:checked) once you tick a row. The open animations come from @starting-style. The whole kit is 164,694 bytes minified, about 23.5 KB gzipped by my measure, close to the 24 KB the README quotes.

The line is who owns the state

Here's the part I think matters beyond this one library.

Look at what each working part rests on. A dialog's open. A popover's :popover-open. A checkbox's :checked. That's state the browser owns. It changes the state when you click, and it tells the accessibility tree about it, because those are native elements with native meaning. CSS only reads the state and paints.

When HTML has no element for the job, CSS can still paint the right picture. What it can't do is change what the page means. Meaning lives in roles and ARIA attributes, and a stylesheet can't write an attribute.

So the rule I'd take from Alloy is this: if the browser owns the state, you don't need JavaScript anymore. If only ARIA can describe the state, you still do.

Dialogs, menus, drawers and disclosures fall on the first side now. Tabs fall on the second.

What a screen reader gets

Alloy's tabs are labels wrapped around radio buttons that share a name. Twelve generated :has() rules show the panel at the same position as the checked radio, so a tab bar tops out at 12 tabs. It works with a mouse, and the arrow keys move between radios. Here's the accessibility tree Chromium built for the tab row after I clicked "Overdue":

- radio "All 24"
- radio "Review them Overdue 3" [checked]
- radio "Paid 10"
- radio "Drafts 2"

Radios, not tabs. The author raised that one himself in the HN thread as the weak spot he knows about. The name on the second radio is one I haven't seen anyone mention. The "Review them" button in the overdue alert above the table isn't a button. It's a <label for="tab-overdue"> styled to look like one, since a label can check a radio from elsewhere on the page with no script. So the button reads as plain text, and its words get glued onto the tab's name.

The bulk bar has a related gap. In the thread, lopis pointed out that a screen reader user never learns the "Selected invoices" bar appeared. I checked: the bar carries no role and no aria-live.

A real tab pattern needs role="tab" and aria-selected flipping as you move. Nothing in CSS can flip it. That's why tabs still need a script, however clever the stylesheet gets. Keithamus, who works on Open UI, noted in the thread that popover itself came out of that group. The fix for tabs looks the same: another native element, not a better hack.

Where else it gets shaky

Your browser floor is higher than the README's headline. It lists Chrome 123, Firefox 125 and Safari 17.5 for the interactive parts, then says dialogs need commandfor, which means Chrome 135, Firefox 144 and Safari 26.2. On older browsers the button that opens a dialog does nothing. The menus lean on position-area, which MDN's compatibility data puts at Chrome 129, Firefox 147 and Safari 26. I didn't test where a menu lands in a browser without it.

The checker checks names, not wiring. Alloy's pitch for AI is a fixed class scale, an llms.txt file, a Claude skill and alloy-check, which lists every class the kit doesn't define. I wrote a test page using only kit classes, by my own tally against alloy.css, with two wiring mistakes: a menu button with popovertarget="sort-menu" pointing at id="sort", and a <div class="dialog"> where a <dialog> belongs. With scripts off, the menu never opened, and the fake dialog sat in plain view from the start. By its source, the checker only scans class attributes, so it would pass that page. I read it; I didn't run it. An AI that writes valid classes on broken markup gets a pass.

The public tests cover the checker, not the CSS. The repo's test folder holds one file with six tests, all for alloy-check. Nothing in the public repo tests that a dialog opens or a panel shows.

And the class names are plain (.button, .dialog, .flex, .hidden), so dropping it into an app with its own CSS will collide, which the README admits and the author confirmed in the thread. It's built for new projects.

Try it

Open the example, then turn scripts off: in Chrome DevTools, press Cmd+Shift+P (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows), type "Disable JavaScript" and reload. Click everything. Then open the accessibility pane on the tab row and see what it calls them.

To use it, link one file:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@alloyhtml/css@1/dist/alloy.min.css">

If your app is server-rendered (Rails, Django, Laravel, htmx), the native parts are worth taking as they are. Spend your script, or at least your screen reader testing, where the browser has no element yet: tabs, and anything that should be heard when it appears.

If browsers shipped one more native element next year, which one would delete the most JavaScript from your app?

articles.title: Managing AI Chat Context Without Sending the Entire Conversation
articles.description: On a chat screen, you type a message and get a reply. Keep talking, and it feels like one continuous...
articles.body_html:
On a chat screen, you type a message and get a reply. Keep talking, and it feels like one continuous conversation.

Behind that screen, your app sends your message to a backend. The backend calls an AI provider—the service we use to run the model—and sends the model’s reply back to the app.

Each user message and assistant reply becomes part of the conversation history. The backend stores that history, but still has to decide which parts to include in the next model request.

Say the user’s next message is: “What about the second option?”

That sentence needs context. Which options? What were we comparing? Did the user set any constraints?

So the backend may need to send earlier messages, previous answers, and tool results alongside that short follow-up.

The user sends one sentence. We might send a whole conversation to explain it.

And as the chat grows, that history keeps growing too.

Send everything on every request, and token consumption climbs. Cut too much, and the assistant starts forgetting things the user expects it to remember.

That’s the problem I’m working through in a conversational AI system: how do I reduce token consumption while keeping the relevant context available?

The user expects the conversation to flow. The cost of maintaining it needs to make sense. And the system needs clear rules for what stays in context, what gets compressed, and when.

I ended up implementing an approach I call grow and flush. Getting there meant working through a few other options, because each one solved part of the problem and introduced another.

Engineering. There’s always another “but.” 😅

The starting point: send everything

The most straightforward approach is to pass the entire conversation back to the model on each request.

The model gets the history it might need. We don’t have to decide which messages to leave out.

But consider what happens as the chat continues.

An early message gets sent again on the next request. And the next. And the next. Meanwhile, new messages and tool results keep joining it.

A one-line follow-up can end up carrying a large amount of history.

Even before we reach the model’s context limit, there’s a practical question: how much of that input is helping the current reply, and how much are we repeatedly sending just because it’s there?

So, let’s start cutting it down.

1. Sliding window: keep the latest messages

Keep only the most recent messages.

For example, with a window of eight, we initially send messages 1–8. When message 9 arrives, we send messages 2–9. Then 3–10, and so on.

Each new message pushes the oldest one out.

Simple enough. The number of messages we send stays small.

The problem

Recent doesn’t always mean relevant.

Suppose the user sets a budget in message 2. At message 10, they ask us to compare something using that same budget.

Message 2 has already left the window.

The user remembers the conversation. The assistant is working with a smaller slice of it.

From the user’s side, that feels like: “We literally just discussed this.”

And honestly, fair.

The old message might still be in the database, but it won’t help the current reply unless we bring it back into the model’s context.

A sliding window can be enough for short chats or exchanges that don’t depend much on earlier messages. For the conversations I needed to support, it left too much behind.

A smaller prompt helps with cost. Making users repeat their instructions adds friction to the product.

We need to preserve something from those older messages.

2. Summarize once, then keep going

What if we summarize the older messages before removing them?

Once the conversation reaches a certain point, we make a summary of the older part and keep the newer messages unchanged.

For example, at message 16:

  • Summarize messages 1–8.
  • Keep messages 9–16 in their original form.
  • Send the summary alongside those recent messages.

From that point, keep appending new messages after the same summary.

Now the assistant has a compact version of the early conversation. Nice.

The problem

The summary stays small. The messages after it keep growing.

At message 20, we’re sending the summary plus messages 9–20.

At message 30, it’s the same summary plus messages 9–30.

We’ve reduced the history once, but the amount of context we send keeps climbing again.

So yes, we’ve bought some breathing room. The token problem is still coming back.

That initial saving doesn’t give us a lasting way to control the cost of a long conversation.

The summary needs to keep moving with the chat.

3. Rolling summary + sliding window

Keep the recent messages in their original form and maintain a summary of the older ones.

As the window moves, merge whatever is leaving it into the existing summary.

With an eight-message window, message 9 pushes message 1 into the summary. Message 10 pushes message 2 into it. The summary grows in coverage while the recent window stays at eight.

That gives us two useful things: recent detail and compressed history.

The raw conversation no longer grows forever. Earlier context has somewhere to go.

The problem

If we update the summary every turn, we’ve added another model call to every turn that needs compaction.

And the summarizer also consumes tokens. It doesn’t run on vibes.

Those calls have their own input and output tokens. Across many active conversations, that adds work and cost just to maintain the memory.

There’s also the timing. If the reply waits for summarization, the user waits. If summarization happens in the background, we need to handle requests arriving before it finishes.

Then there’s repeated compression. An older detail has to survive every rewrite of the summary.

“Keep the budget under $500, including delivery” might eventually become “user has a limited budget.”

That’s quite a different instruction.

A summary that changes every turn can also reduce how much of the prompt remains reusable through prompt caching. The effect depends on where the summary sits and how the provider handles caching.

Maybe we can keep this structure and summarize less often.

4. Batch the summaries. Meet the amnesia gap.

Keep the eight-message window, but wait until six messages have left it before summarizing them together.

That gives us fewer summary calls.

Sounds reasonable. Until we look at what happens while those six messages are accumulating.

The problem

At message 9, message 1 has left the window. But we haven’t summarized it yet.

At message 13, messages 1–5 are waiting for the batch threshold.

They’re in neither the summary nor the raw messages being sent to the model.

At message 14, six messages have accumulated, so we finally trigger summarization.

That waiting period is the amnesia gap. A temporary black hole for context. 💀

Those messages might be safely stored somewhere. The model still can’t use them for the current reply.

If the user refers to something in that gap, the assistant is missing the very context we were planning to preserve.

This is where the system’s internal scheduling starts showing up as a product problem. The assistant can appear to forget something, then have access to it again after the summary catches up.

The gap exists before the summarization call even starts. A slow or failed call can make it last longer.

Batching helps with summary frequency. Evicting messages while they wait for the batch creates the problem.

That led to the next change.

5. Grow and flush

Keep the waiting messages in the prompt.

Instead of forcing the raw window to stay at eight, let it grow until there’s enough older material to summarize together.

Using eight and sixteen as example thresholds:

  1. Keep the original messages while the buffer grows.
  2. When it reaches 16, summarize the older eight.
  3. Once the summary is successfully saved, remove those eight from the active prompt.
  4. Retain the recent eight and let the buffer grow again.

That’s grow and flush.

On the first flush, messages 1–8 become the summary. Messages 9–16 stay in their original form.

As new messages arrive, we send that same summary plus messages 9–17, then 9–18, and so on.

At message 24, we combine the previous summary with messages 9–16. The updated summary covers messages 1–16, while messages 17–24 stay raw.

The buffer grows, then shrinks. The summary advances in batches.

The important rule is:

Keep a segment in its original form until a successfully saved summary covers it.

The messages waiting for compaction remain available to the model. They don’t disappear while we wait for the batch threshold.

“Flush” here means removing messages from the active prompt. It doesn’t require deleting the stored transcript.

If compaction runs after a response finishes, that response still uses the expanded raw buffer. Later requests can use the new summary once it has been saved.

A background job can’t go back and help a reply that already happened. Sadly, no time travel included.

The problem

We’ve given the buffer room to grow, so the main prompt is sometimes larger than it would be with a strict sliding window.

That’s the trade: fewer summary updates, more original messages carried between updates.

Fewer summary calls don’t automatically mean a lower total bill. The extra raw context costs tokens too.

The useful comparison includes the main requests, the summarization requests, summary size, and any cache savings.

The goal is to find a balance that keeps the conversation useful at a sensible operating cost.

How the approaches compare

Approach Main benefit Raw context Summary updates Main tradeoff
Sliding window Simple; no summarization calls Fixed recent window None Older context drops out
One-time summary Compresses early history while retaining a summary Grows after the summary point Once Token growth returns
Rolling summary + window Keeps recent detail alongside summarized history Fixed recent window Every turn that moves the window Frequent calls and repeated compression
Batched summary + fixed window Reduces summary frequency Fixed recent window After enough evictions Waiting messages fall into a gap
Grow and flush Batches updates while retaining messages awaiting compaction Grows, then shrinks After enough retained messages accumulate Larger prompts between flushes

Why grow and flush works for us

Grow and flush fits our current needs because it lets us batch summary updates while keeping the waiting messages available. Recent exchanges also stay in their original form, so the model gets their detail directly.

That gives us the balance we’re after: less frequent summarization, recent detail, and no amnesia gap caused by premature eviction.

In the simplified grow-and-flush example, compaction happens once per eight new messages after the initial warm-up.

Between flushes, the summary stays unchanged and new messages append to the raw history. That creates an opportunity to reuse a stable prompt prefix.

Caching can reduce processing cost. The cached content still occupies context, though. We still need to manage its size.

The tradeoffs I still need to account for

A summary can lose an important detail.

Grow and flush prevents the gap caused by dropping messages before they’ve been summarized. It doesn’t make summaries lossless.

It also still rewrites an existing summary, just less often. We need to check whether constraints, exact values, corrections, and unfinished work survive those updates.

Compaction involves choosing what to preserve. Something that looks unimportant now might matter later.

Message counts aren’t token limits.

Eight short messages and eight pasted documents are very different amounts of input.

One user pastes a giant log, and suddenly “it’s only eight messages” isn’t so comforting.

A possible solution is to use two triggers and compact when either threshold is reached:

  • The unsummarized buffer reaches the message-count limit, such as 16 messages.
  • Its estimated token size reaches the token budget, even if there are fewer messages.

Whichever comes first.

That way, a few large messages can trigger compaction before the buffer reaches the message-count limit.

The amount we retain after compaction also needs to fit the budget. Keeping the latest eight is a useful target, but eight enormous messages could still be too much.

We also need to check the full request size, leaving room for instructions, tools, the summary, and the response. A single oversized message may need separate handling.

And messages aren’t the same as complete turns. One user request can produce several assistant and tool messages.

Background compaction can fall behind.

While an update is pending, keep the unsummarized messages available.

Before sending the next request, check whether the full context still fits. If it doesn’t, the system needs a fallback, such as waiting for compaction or reducing oversized content.

The summary and its boundary need to stay in sync.

We need to save both the summary and the point in the transcript it covers.

If those disagree, messages can be skipped or unnecessarily repeated. Overlapping jobs also need protection so an older update doesn’t overwrite a newer one.

Critical action state needs reliable storage.

A pending confirmation or an exact action parameter should live in application state.

The summary helps the assistant follow the conversation. The action flow still needs a reliable source of truth.

For me, this is where the Product, Business, and System concerns meet: the conversation should feel continuous, the cost should remain sensible, and the implementation should behave predictably when work is delayed or fails.

Bonus: don’t cut a tool exchange in half

This applies whenever we trim or summarize conversation history.

An assistant can issue a tool call and then receive a matching result. A blind cut at “the last eight messages” can separate that result from its call.

Summarization can create the same split. If the tool call gets absorbed into the summary while its result stays in the raw history, the next request contains a result without its matching structured call.

Mentioning the call in a text summary doesn’t replace the original tool-call message.

Parallel calls make the boundary more interesting: one assistant message may need several matching results.

Depending on the API, an incomplete exchange can produce an invalid request.

When trimming or choosing a chunk to summarize, preserve complete tool exchanges, including the matching IDs and required results. Compact a completed exchange together, and keep unfinished exchanges protected in the raw context.

All that thought about memory, only to trip over one bad slice. Lovely. 😅

Where I’m taking this next

Grow and flush is what I’ve implemented for this problem.

It gives me a clear rule for when history can leave the prompt, while allowing summary updates to happen in batches.

I’m still investigating better ways to preserve useful context with less token consumption. Structured memory, selective retrieval, and different compaction schedules are all worth exploring.

If you’ve worked through this, I’d like to hear what worked, what broke, and what you’d change here. Suggestions are welcome.

articles.title: Why "rm -rf $D*" Bypasses Almost Every AI Guardrail (And How We Scanned 115k Lines of Production Code)
articles.description: Traditional AI safety guardrails match text strings using regex. But operating systems execute resolved shell commands. Here is why 11 out of 11 commercial agents failed GuardFall, and the open-source AST engine we built to fix it.
articles.body_html:
Look at this bash command for a moment:

D=/; rm -rf $D*

If you feed that string into almost any commercial AI safety filter, prompt guardrail, or regex-based security rule, it reports:

[Guardrail Status]: PASS (SAFE)
Reason: No literal "/" root directory path detected.

Now ask your operating system's kernel to run it.

Before the command reaches the kernel, bash performs parameter expansion. $D expands to /. The string becomes:

rm -rf /*

The shell executes a recursive wipe of your entire operating system storage.

This is not a hypothetical bug. In the GuardFall academic benchmark published on June 30, 2026, researchers tested pre-execution command guards across 11 actively maintained autonomous coding agents spanning roughly 548,000 GitHub stars.

Almost every single agent failed.

Goose leaked on 22 of 23 bypass cases. OpenCode leaked on 16 of 16. Guardrails were checking what the command looked like. The operating system was executing what the command actually expanded into.

Here is why this disconnect happens, what happened when we pointed an AST resolver at 115,000 lines of viral open-source code, and how we built an open-source flight simulator to fix it.

1. The Fundamental Flaw: String Matching vs. Shell Expansion

Most agent guardrails today treat shell commands as plain text. They compile a list of "forbidden substrings":

  • rm -rf /
  • DROP TABLE
  • chmod 777
  • mkfs 
  Traditional Guardrail:
  [ AI Output String ] ──( Regex Text Match )──▶ "Looks harmless" ──▶ PASS
                                                                         │
                                                                         ▼
                                                            [ KERNEL EXECUTION ]
                                                            `rm -rf /*` (WIPED)

The problem is that POSIX shells do not execute strings—they compile them through an evaluation pipeline:

  1. Quote Removal: "r""m" -rf / has zero literal rm substring, but evaluates to rm.
  2. Parameter Expansion: D=/; rm -rf $D* disguises the root path in an environment variable.
  3. Command Substitution: rm -rf $(echo /) dynamically generates the path at runtime.
  4. Subshell Assembly: bash -c "rm -rf /" wraps execution in a child process that evades parent text filters.
  5. Pipeline Piping: cat script.sh | sh reads an arbitrary unreviewed script directly into an interpreter.

A guard evaluating the pre-transformation string and an operating system executing the post-transformation string are evaluating two completely different commands.

To secure an autonomous coding agent, you cannot use regular expressions. You must parse the shell's Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and resolve expansions statically before applying policy.

2. The Second Crisis: The "MCP Token Tax"

While solving the command evasion problem, we hit an equally devastating bottleneck in the agent ecosystem: Model Context Protocol (MCP) context bloat.

When you connect an autonomous agent (like Cursor or Claude Code) to 8–10 enterprise MCP servers (PostgreSQL, GitHub, Docker, filesystem, Slack), the client injects every single tool schema into the system prompt.

  Without BlastRadius:
  Prompt = [Your 20-word question] + [30,000 tokens of dead schema JSON]
  Cost: $0.30 per query in pure schema overhead
  Latency: 4–8 seconds inference lag
  Hallucination: High (model forgets user instructions)
  • The Financial Impact: At 1,000 agent loops per day, a team burns $9,000 to $80,000 per month just paying for static JSON schemas the model doesn't even use in that turn!
  • The Cognitive Impact: Large language models suffer from "attention dilution." Stuffing 30,000 tokens of schemas causes the agent to hallucinate, ignore negative constraints, and forget project instructions.

3. What We Built: BlastRadius-Zero (v2.0)

We spent the last few months engineering a zero-dependency, local-first runtime for autonomous agents called BlastRadius-Zero (blastradius-mcp).

It sits between the agent and your system, functioning like an in-memory flight simulator:

It operates across 4 core architectural pillars:

Pillar 1: The Swarm Pre-Flight Safety Simulator

Before any command executes or any Pull Request merges, BlastRadius unleashes 50 virtual adversarial personas in < 50 milliseconds in-memory:

  • The Hacker: Tests SQL injection, authentication bypasses, and secret harvesting.
  • The Concurrency Racer: Provokes race conditions, deadlocks, and simultaneous state mutations.
  • The Confused User: Injects invalid parameters, skipped steps, and rapid re-triggers.
  • The Legacy System: Simulates latency spikes, stale cache returns, and dropped connections.
  • The Data Corruptor: Injects Unicode edge cases, null bytes, and schema mismatches.

It outputs a color-coded Blast Heatmap (0–100 Danger Score). If an action scores high risk, execution is physically halted before system state is touched.

Pillar 2: Shell AST Static Resolution

It tokenizes shell input, resolves quotes, variable assignments, and subshell wrappers, reconstructing the exact command the kernel will execute. It catches all 23 GuardFall shell bypass classes that fool standard regex filters.

Pillar 3: Zero-Bloat JIT Gateway (99.4% Token Reduction)

Instead of stuffing 50 tool schemas into prompt memory, BlastRadius exposes one single intelligent dispatcher tool (route_tool).

  • Tool schemas are fetched Just-In-Time only when needed.
  • Large tool returns (e.g. 50KB database tables) are compressed into virtual references (ctx_981a) with automated PII and API key redaction.
  • Result: Slashes prompt context overhead from 9,522 tokens down to 55 tokens (a 99.4% context cut).

Pillar 4: Autonomous TDD State Lock

Autonomous agents love writing code without tests or swallowing errors in empty try {} catch {} blocks. BlastRadius physically enforces a Red $\rightarrow$ Green $\rightarrow$ Refactor lock: the agent cannot touch production files until it writes a failing test proving the change, makes it pass, and eliminates anti-patterns.

4. The 115,000 LOC Stress Test: What Happened When We Scanned 12 Viral Repos

We didn't want to test this on toy benchmarks. We pointed our engine at 115,000 lines of production code across 12 of the most popular open-source repositories in the world:

  • expressjs/express
  • axios/axios
  • fastify/fastify
  • motdotla/dotenv
  • winstonjs/winston
  • Automattic/mongoose
  • ...and 6 others.

The Results:

  • Execution Time: 2.62 seconds total.
  • Passing Test Suite: 237 out of 237 automated tests passing with zero mocks on security logic.
  • Issues Uncovered: 446 real-world vulnerabilities and code smells, including:
    • 32 completely empty try/catch blocks that silently swallow fatal runtime errors.
    • 30 dangerous shell sinks that concatenate untrusted input into child processes.
    • 84 unbounded async promises with missing rejection handlers.
    • 14 credential leaks in test fixtures that could be harvested by adversarial agents.

5. Try It Right Now (Zero Install, 100% Local)

BlastRadius-Zero is completely open-source under Apache-2.0.

It runs on Node 22+ (leveraging native node:sqlite in WAL mode). It opens no network sockets, sends zero telemetry to the cloud, requires no API keys, and has no paid tier.

You can run it in your terminal right now in 5 seconds:

npx -y blastradius-mcp

Adding to Cursor or VS Code

Add it to your MCP configuration (mcpServers):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "blastradius": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "blastradius-mcp"]
    }
  }
}

6. The Bottom Line

Autonomous AI coding agents are the future of software engineering. But letting an agent execute arbitrary shell commands with regex guardrails is like flying a rocket without a pre-flight checklist.

If you are building with Cursor, Claude Code, Cline, or custom agent frameworks, protect your machine and your team's production database before letting agents loose.

⭐ Check out the code, read our 23-bypass test suite, and star the repo on GitHub:

👉 github.com/Jimil-Joshi/blastradius-mcp

(PRs, edge cases, and adversarial persona contributions are very welcome!)

articles.title: What AI coding agents install, and what they skip
articles.description: I gave Claude, GPT, Gemini and 8 open models the same 100 build tasks. Sentry and Playwright win every time. Datadog: named 28 times, installed 0.
articles.body_html:
I build something almost every day, and these days an AI agent writes most of the code. Again and again I watched it choose the tools for me: the login library, the database, the email API. I never named one. It typed npm install, and that was the decision.

I kept asking myself three things. Why this one? Would another model pick something else? And is there a better tool out there that I never see, because I'm stuck with the model's choice?

So I started measuring it. Here's what came out of 2,188 answers from 11 models.

How I measured it

  • 100 build tasks in 20 categories: auth, hosted Postgres, ORM, payments, email, hosting, file storage, job queues, cron, feature flags, error monitoring, analytics, logging, search, vector databases, LLM tracing, CMS, realtime, end-to-end tests and UI components. They read like real requests and never name a product. One of them: "I need a hosted Postgres database for my Next.js side project. Pick one, set it up and connect to it."
  • One short system prompt for every model: you're a coding agent in the user's project, make the technical choices yourself.
  • Each task twice per model, temperature 1.0, through the public APIs.
  • Run 1 (2 Nov): Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.6 Terra and Gemini 3.1 Pro. 600 answers.
  • Run 2 (16 Nov): 8 open-weight models: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen3 Coder Next, GLM 5.3, Kimi K2, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, gpt-oss-120b, Devstral 2 and Gemma 4 31B. 1,588 answers.
  • The pick is what gets installed: the install command first, then package.json, then the imports. A product the answer only talks about doesn't count. 60 random answers per run were checked one by one against the pick.
  • Both runs cost under $10 in API calls.

Some categories are already decided

Sentry for error monitoring and Playwright for end-to-end tests went into all 30 answers from Claude, GPT and Gemini. The open models mostly agree: Sentry in 76 of 80 answers, Playwright in 66 of 80.

In 9 of the 20 categories, one product won more than half of the big three's answers: Stripe for payments (24 of 30), Neon for Postgres (20), Drizzle over Prisma (16 to 5), Resend for email (16).

The bottom of the list matters too. Auth, feature flags and realtime have no clear winner, so there the pick still depends on the model and on how you ask.

Named isn't installed

The number I find most useful is the gap between being mentioned and being installed.

  • Supabase came up in 4 of the 30 hosted Postgres answers and was installed in none. Neon got 20. Claude, right after installing Neon's driver: "If you'd rather have auth and storage bundled too, Supabase is the alternative."
  • Datadog was named in 9 logging answers and installed in 0. The agents set up Grafana and Prometheus (12) or OpenTelemetry (10).
  • Cloudflare R2 was named 6 times, usually as "the same code with a different endpoint". The install was AWS S3 every time.
  • Mailgun was named 4 times and never installed. Resend got 16.

The open models make it even clearer. Across all 11 models, Datadog was named in 28 answers and installed in none. Mailgun: named 27 times, installed 0. R2: 14 and 0. (Supabase does better there: the open models installed it 6 times out of 80.)

A mention shows the agent knows the market. The install is the decision.

The models don't agree

Auth is the clearest case. Claude reached for Auth.js. Gemini went to Clerk. GPT wrote its own login, with sessions and password hashing, in 4 of its 10 answers.

It goes beyond auth. Claude never installed Prisma; Gemini did 4 times out of 10. GPT kept vectors in Postgres with pgvector 6 times out of 10; Gemini never did. So "what AI recommends" depends on which AI.

The open models: same defaults, three real differences

Then I ran the same 100 tasks on 8 open-weight models. I expected a different world. It mostly isn't: they install the same first pick as Claude, GPT and Gemini in 17 of the 20 categories.

The three where they don't:

  • Feature flags: Unleash first (31%). The big three go to PostHog (33%), which the open models pick only 16% of the time.
  • Logging: OpenTelemetry first (51%), not Grafana and Prometheus.
  • LLM tracing: LangSmith first (33%), Langfuse 22%. And in 38% of these answers they built the tracing themselves.

Two more patterns:

  • They build it by hand more often: 14% of all answers, against 9%. In feature flags, 28% of their answers rolled their own. In file storage, 41% installed no storage service at all; most just took the upload with Multer.
  • Single models have strong habits. Devstral 2 picked Cypress for end-to-end tests in 7 of 10 answers, where the big three never did. gpt-oss-120b sent email over plain SMTP with Nodemailer in 8 of 10. Gemma 4 picked LangSmith in 7 of 10. Qwen3 Coder and Kimi K2 went to OpenTelemetry in 8 of 10.

What I take from it

As a builder, I've stopped taking the default for granted. The model's first pick is often good. It isn't always the best tool for my case, so when it matters, I name the tool myself. And if you switch models, expect a slightly different stack from each.

If you make a dev tool, part of your funnel now runs through an agent that types the install command for the user. That reader doesn't see your landing page. It sees your package name, your docs and how short your setup is. Neon's driver goes in with one line, and the models describe Supabase as a bigger platform. That's true, and it's why Supabase ends up as the alternative and not the default.

The limits

  • These are API answers, not agents working inside a real repo with its own files and history. What's already installed would change things.
  • About 30 answers per category for the big three and 80 for the open models. Treat a gap of a few points as a tie.
  • Models change every few months, so every number carries its run date.

The data

Every prompt and every raw answer is public, free to reuse under CC BY 4.0:

  • One short write-up per finding
  • Open models vs Claude, GPT and Gemini, category by category
  • The method and the raw data

If a number looks wrong to you, say so in the comments. I'd rather fix the data than defend it.

And I'm curious: what did your agent install for you lately that you didn't expect?

I wrote this with help from my AI assistant, which also runs the benchmark. Every number comes from the published data linked above.

articles.title: Resetting Vue State When Related Converter Routes Reuse One Component
articles.description: Moving between two converter URLs does not necessarily mean Vue creates a fresh component instance....
articles.body_html:
Moving between two converter URLs does not necessarily mean Vue creates a fresh component instance. I'll use a feet-to-meters page to show how to reset reused input refs without letting two-way watchers overwrite the intended defaults.

I used a feet-to-meters page as a concrete example. The arithmetic is simply multiplication by 0.3048, but the implementation is more interesting as a small case study in route-driven data, editable state, and resetting both sides of a two-way calculation.

Put Page Identity in Route Data

The application describes fixed conversion pairs as data. Each pair carries a slug, category, source unit, destination unit, development-order value, and localized content.

The router expands those definitions into routes that use one shared component. It places the pair slug in route metadata, so the component can look up the current definition:

const pair = computed(() => getPairBySlug(route.meta.slug));

The lookup function is deliberately small:

export function getPairBySlug(slug) {
  return allConverterPairs.find((p) => p.slug === slug);
}

For the feet-to-meters page, the selected definition uses ft and m. Another route can select a different pair without requiring a second copy of the input template or synchronization functions.

The important distinction is between page identity and component identity. The URL and metadata identify a different conversion, while Vue may still be rendering the same component type. The app renders the routed component without a URL-based key, so navigation between these pair pages can reuse its instance. A setup-time read copied into a plain constant would not express that changing relationship.

Using a computed lookup means the displayed pair can follow the reactive route metadata. It does not, by itself, reset every editable ref owned by the component. That second responsibility needs its own code.

Reset Both Fields Before Recomputing

The component begins with a left value of 1, a right value of zero, and a synchronization guard. It watches the pair slug:

watch(
  () => route.meta.slug,
  () => {
    isSyncing = true;
    fromValue.value = 1;
    toValue.value = 0;
    isSyncing = false;
    syncFromLeft();
  },
);

This defines a clear navigation policy: moving to another pair starts that pair with a source value of 1. It does not carry an arbitrary measurement from the previous page into a new set of units.

Why assign both fields while the guard is active? Both refs have synchronous watchers. Without the outer guard, assigning 1 to the source could immediately update the destination. The next reset assignment, setting the destination to zero, would then trigger a reverse conversion and overwrite the source with zero. The final left-to-right synchronization would convert that zero, not the intended 1.

The guarded reset writes the defaults without treating either write as a new user edit. After releasing the guard, it deliberately performs one left-to-right synchronization using the current pair.

That final call is important. Merely resetting the destination to zero would leave the UI showing a placeholder rather than a valid conversion. On the feet-to-meters route, one foot should produce 0.3048 meters.

This is a product choice as well as a reactive detail. Another application might preserve the last entered physical length across navigation, but that would require defining which unit gives that saved magnitude meaning. Preserving an unlabeled number is not the same as preserving a measurement.

Keep User Edits Separate from Derived Writes

The shared left-side synchronization function reads the current pair at the moment it calculates:

function syncFromLeft() {
  if (isSyncing || !pair.value) return;
  isSyncing = true;
  toValue.value = categoryConfig.value.round(
    categoryConfig.value.convert(fromValue.value, pair.value.from, pair.value.to),
  );
  isSyncing = false;
}

The reverse function swaps the unit keys and writes the source field. Both value watchers use synchronous flushing:

watch(fromValue, syncFromLeft, { flush: "sync" });
watch(toValue, syncFromRight, { flush: "sync" });

That means the guard is still active when a programmatic write invokes the opposite watcher. The boolean depends on this timing: changing these watchers to deferred execution would require revisiting the guard, because it would already be false when queued callbacks ran.

That protects directionality. If the user types six feet, the left value is authoritative and the right side becomes 1.8288 meters. If the user instead edits the meters field, that value becomes authoritative for the reverse calculation.

The category configuration selects the correct conversion and rounding functions. For length pairs, those functions use the shared meter-based scales and round output to at most six decimal places. The component does not need a feet-to-meters-specific watcher.

An initial syncFromLeft() also runs during setup. The first server-rendered result can therefore contain the correct conversion instead of waiting for a browser mount hook to replace zero. That initialization serves a different purpose from the route-change watcher: one establishes the first result, and the other handles later pair changes.

I find this separation easier to test than relying on a forced component remount for every navigation. The reset policy is visible in the component, and the same arithmetic path serves initialization, navigation, and ordinary edits.

Define What Should Survive Navigation

The watcher observes route.meta.slug, not every route change. An in-app language change that keeps the same pair slug is not, by this watcher alone, an instruction to reset the measurement. The localized content is computed separately from the pair and current locale. This does not promise persistence across a full page load: a new component instance starts from its setup defaults.

There are limits to the data lookup too. getPairBySlug returns undefined when no entry matches. Some synchronization code guards against a missing pair, but other setup expressions assume registered route data exists. The component is designed for the router's generated definitions, not as a complete arbitrary-slug error page.

The six-decimal rounding policy also remains in effect after navigation. For example, 0.000001 feet converts to 0.0000003048 meters, which rounds to zero here. The factor 0.3048 is exact by definition, but JavaScript floating-point arithmetic and output rounding still impose limits. A reset does not improve numerical precision, and retaining an edited value would not restore digits already rounded away.

I checked the component's conversion block with actual Vue refs and watchers, using reactive route metadata and a synthetic reverse-pair fixture. Entering 2 meters kept that edited field at 2 and produced 6.56168 feet. After changing the slug and awaiting nextTick(), the source reset to 1; returning to feet-to-meters produced 0.3048 meters. Replacing the metadata with the same slug preserved the edited values. Removing only the reset guard made a pair change end at zero on both sides.

Those are component-state checks, not browser navigation or localization tests. I'd still test the rendered labels and the actual language-switching flow separately; keeping a slug unchanged only establishes that this particular watcher should not reset the fields.

I turned this into a small free tool: Feet to Meters Converter.

articles.title: Rails + Rspack: esbuild speed, webpack features, one command
articles.description: Why I went looking   I wanted one thing from my Rails frontend setup: change a file and see...
articles.body_html:
Why I went looking

I wanted one thing from my Rails frontend setup: change a file and see it on the page, without losing where I was.

esbuild through jsbundling-rails gets close. Builds are fast and the config is one line. But every change is a full page reload. The modal I opened, the form I half filled, the Stimulus controller's state: gone, every time. Over a day of UI work that adds up to hundreds of small resets.

Webpacker and Shakapacker give you hot module replacement, but I remember what came with it. A config you are scared to touch, cold builds measured in tens of seconds, and upgrades that meant diffing generated files by hand.

Rspack promised both: webpack's features, including HMR, with a Rust core that builds at esbuild speed. So I tried it on a Rails app, and then I wrapped what I learned into a gem, rspack_rails.

The first ten minutes

A new app is three commands:

rails new myapp -m https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tungnt1203/rspack_rails/main/template.rb
cd myapp
bin/dev

The template asks which extras you want: Stimulus, TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, Sass. bin/dev starts Rails and rspack serve side by side.

Then the part that sold me. I edited a Stimulus controller, and the page did not reload. The controller was swapped in place, and the element I was poking at kept its state. Same with CSS, and with React components through Fast Refresh. When I edited an ERB view, the page reloaded on its own, which is what you want for server-rendered HTML.

The layout needs only two helpers:

<%= rspack_javascript_tag "application", "data-turbo-track": "reload" %>
<%= rspack_stylesheet_tag "application" %>

An existing app is bundle add rspack_rails and bin/rails rspack:install. An app on importmap-rails or jsbundling-rails can run bin/rails rspack:migrate from a clean git tree and review the diff.

The numbers

Rspack is not the fastest at everything, and I think that is the honest headline. esbuild still wins a cold build, by a few hundred milliseconds. Rspack wins the number you feel all day: the rebuild after you save a file.

Measured on an Apple M1, Node 26. Medians of 5 cold builds and 10 watch rebuilds, November 2026.

A rebuild after editing one component took 83 ms with Rspack and 279 ms with esbuild, on 1,000 components. Cold development builds were a tie between the two (0.55 s and 0.54 s), with webpack at 1.46 s. Against webpack, Rspack's production build is 6 to 9 times faster.

And the rebuild number undersells it. esbuild has no HMR, so after its rebuild the browser still reloads the whole page. Rspack sends only the changed module.

How I measured: the same generated React 19 + TypeScript app (lodash-es, date-fns), built to ES2022 with source maps. esbuild runs with the flags jsbundling-rails uses, plus --minify. webpack 5 uses swc-loader, as Shakapacker can. Times include about 0.2 s of npx and Node startup. Gzipped output was 100 KB for Rspack and webpack, 120 KB for esbuild.

The proxy rspack_rails puts in front of the dev server costs about 1.8 ms per page navigation.

What I learned building the gem

Getting Rspack to run in Rails takes an afternoon. Getting it to stay out of your way took the rest. Four decisions mattered most.

Production stays boring. Rspack writes to app/assets/builds, and Propshaft or Sprockets fingerprints and serves the files, the same way jsbundling-rails works. Production never needs Node at runtime, and there is no second manifest system to debug at 2 a.m.

The dev server hides behind Rails. Pages load scripts from /rspack/... on the app's own origin, and Rails proxies them to rspack serve. I learned why the hard way: browsers refuse to start a Web Worker from another origin, so loading straight from localhost:3036 breaks workers. Only the HMR websocket talks to the dev server directly.

The config is owned, not generated once. Webpacker's pain was a config generated on install and never upgraded again. Here the base config, config/rspack/rails.mjs, belongs to the gem and is rewritten on every upgrade. Your changes live in a callback in rspack.config.mjs. If someone edits the gem's file by hand, a checksum notices and the edit is backed up before anything is replaced.

A doctor that tells you what to type. bin/rails rspack:doctor checks Node.js, packages, config, layouts, Procfile.dev, the Dockerfile and the dev server. Every warning ends with the command that fixes it. It is the first thing I run when something looks off.

The bugs that taught me the most came from real apps, not tests. Migrating an app with two layouts showed that the admin layout silently lost its JavaScript. That fix shipped in 1.0.0.rc2.

When you should not use it

If your app has a few Stimulus controllers and no npm packages that need bundling, stay on importmap-rails. It is the Rails default for good reasons: no Node, no build step, nothing to learn.

If you bundle but never miss HMR, esbuild through jsbundling-rails is a fine choice. It is simple, very fast on cold builds, and has fewer moving parts than any webpack-style tool.

rspack_rails is for the point where you want more than that: React or TypeScript with Fast Refresh, code splitting, CSS modules, loaders, or the webpack plugin you already know. That is where I kept wishing for webpack's features without webpack's wait.

Try it

rspack_rails 1.0 is on RubyGems. It supports Rails 7.2 and 8.x, Propshaft and Sprockets, and npm, Yarn, pnpm and bun.

rails new myapp -m https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tungnt1203/rspack_rails/main/template.rb
  • Code and docs: github.com/tungnt1203/rspack_rails
  • Demo app: rspack_rails-demo

If you try it on a real app, I would love to hear what broke. The best fixes so far came from exactly that. Open an issue, or tell me in the comments.

articles.title: The sign is where bank statement parsers break: -64.28 DR, (123.45), 100.00 CR
articles.description: Bank statements are the one PDF most people are told to 'just convert', and the one they should be...
articles.body_html:
Bank statements are the one PDF most people are told to 'just convert', and the one they should be most careful about handing to a website. A statement is a complete account history: account number, every payer and vendor, every balance. I wanted to see how far a good parser could get with the file never leaving the machine, so I built one as a single page and kept the parsing rules explicit.

This is what actually decides whether the CSV is right or wrong.

Why parse in the browser

The file goes: FileReader → ArrayBuffer → pdfjsLib.getDocument({data}) → page.getTextContent() → my parser → Blob → download. There is no fetch, no upload endpoint, no analytics event. The trade-off is honest: no OCR, no server-side PDF toolbox, and any really broken layout stays broken. In exchange, 'what happens to my statement?' has a one-word answer.

Five spellings of the same debit

A statement writes money going out in at least five ways, and they are not interchangeable to a spreadsheet:

  • -64.28 — a minus sign
  • 64.28 DR — the bank debit marker, no minus
  • (123.45) — accounting parentheses
  • −64.28 — the Unicode minus (U+2212), which is not the hyphen
  • 100.00 CR — a credit, so positive

The classic bug is inverting a sign twice: treat DR as negative and then honour a minus that is already there, or flip parentheses and then negate again. One $64 purchase becomes a $64 deposit, and reconciliation is off by $128 for that row. So the rule is: decide the sign once.

function cleanAmount(value) {
  if (value == null) return null;
  let s = String(value).trim();
  s = s.split('$').join('').split(',').join('')
       .split(String.fromCharCode(0x2212)).join('-');
  let negative = false;

  if (s.startsWith('(') && s.endsWith(')')) { negative = true; s = s.slice(1, -1).trim(); }

  const upper = s.toUpperCase();
  if (upper.endsWith('DR')) { negative = true; s = s.slice(0, -2).trim(); }
  else if (upper.endsWith('CR')) { s = s.slice(0, -2).trim(); }

  if (s.startsWith('-')) { negative = true; s = s.slice(1).trim(); }
  else if (s.startsWith('+')) { s = s.slice(1).trim(); }

  if (s === '' || isNaN(Number(s))) return null;
  const n = parseFloat(s);
  return negative ? -n : n;
}

Note the order: strip the marker, then the explicit sign, then apply the negative flag once at the end.

PDF text is not lines

getTextContent() gives you items with a transform matrix; each item has an x (matrix[4]) and a y (matrix[5]). Rebuild lines yourself:

const buckets = [];
for (const it of items) {
  if (!it.str) continue;
  const x = it.transform[4];
  const y = it.transform[5];
  let b = buckets.find(b => Math.abs(b.y - y) <= 2.5);
  if (!b) { b = { y, items: [] }; buckets.push(b); }
  b.items.push({ x, s: it.str });
}
buckets.sort((a, b) => b.y - a.y);          // top to bottom
const lines = buckets.map(b => b.items
  .sort((a, b) => a.x - b.x)                // left to right
  .map(i => i.s).join(' '));

The 2.5 tolerance is the part that needs patience: too tight and one line splits in two, too loose and two transactions merge.

Two layouts, one parser

Some banks print one transaction per line:

10/02/2026  ONLINE PAYMENT TO ADOBE INC   -54.99   4,945.01

Others print one column per line:

10/07/2026
CARD PURCHASE STAPLES #1123
64.28 DR
7,380.73

Both are handled by grouping lines into blocks that start at a date, and stopping collection once the block already holds two amounts. Without that stop, the footer closing balance gets appended to the last transaction, and the running balance is wrong for exactly the rows people check first.

Within a block, if there are two or more numbers, the last is the balance and the first non-zero one before it is the transaction. The description is whatever is left after removing the matched amounts.

Fail loudly on scans

An image-only PDF produces zero characters of text. The friendly-looking bug is to show an empty table, which reads as 'your statement has no transactions'. The tool checks the extracted character count and says what is actually true: no selectable text layer — run OCR first, or download the PDF version from your bank.

The regex bug worth naming

My amount pattern was:

/[0-9]{1,3}(?:,[0-9]{3})*[.][0-9]{2}/

For 1,850.00 it matches all of it. For 1850.00 — an ordinary way to print four digits — it matches 850.00, silently. No error, no empty row: a wrong number that looks right.

The fix is an explicit alternation:

/(?:[0-9]{1,3}(?:,[0-9]{3})+[.][0-9]{2}|[0-9]+[.][0-9]{2})/

The grouped form now requires at least one comma; everything else falls back to plain digits. I only found it by writing a test with an ungrouped amount, not by reading the code.

The tests that matter

If you maintain anything like this, this list catches most of the damage:

  1. -64.28, 64.28 DR, (123.45), 100.00 CR, −64.28 resolve to the right sign
  2. a minus plus DR does not flip twice
  3. a split-line block keeps its own balance
  4. amounts with and without thousands separators
  5. CSV quoting for a description containing a comma or a quote
  6. an image-only PDF reports no text layer, not an empty table

Try it

The free page converts up to 20 rows per file and still shows the full transaction count with an in/out/net summary: https://yougkxm.github.io/bank-to-csv/

The desktop version exports every row, writes a formatted .xlsx workbook and batches a folder of statements. Early-bird link: https://8299181964131.gumroad.com/l/bank-statement-to-excel/EARLY50

No OCR, no categorising, no tax logic. It reads electronic statements, gets the sign right once, and tells you when it cannot read the file at all.
